llm-serving-inference-q1.testing: whether you know a request is two different workloads, prefill and decode, with a scheduler in front and a stream behind.
llm-serving-inference-q1.trap: describing it as one forward pass that returns a response object.
llm-serving-inference-q1.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "A request passes through a gateway and a queue, then becomes two different workloads on the GPU: a prefill that reads the whole prompt once, and a decode loop that produces one token per step. The first token appears when prefill ends."
2 · The path, hop by hop "The gateway authenticates, applies the tenant's token rate limit and picks a model. The request waits for admission. Then the server tokenizes, and the scheduler adds it to a batch that is already running. Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel and writes the KV cache. The first decode step samples a token, and it is streamed back as an event."
3 · Prove it "As arithmetic: fifty milliseconds of queue plus a two-thousand-token prompt at five thousand tokens a second gives a time to first token of about four hundred and fifty milliseconds."
4 · What it costs or breaks "Each hop can add to that: a full queue, a prefix-cache miss, a long prompt from another tenant ahead of me, or a proxy that buffers the stream."
5 · So what for the system "So I measure time to first token as queue plus prefill, per stage, and I pull each lever separately: admission control for the queue, prefix caching for the prefill, and no buffering on the way out."
Close "Gateway, queue, prefill, first decode step, stream: five hops, and each one has its own failure."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"Prefill and decode are different machines that happen to share a GPU."

Prefill Decode
Work all prompt tokens in one parallel pass one new token per step
Bound by compute memory bandwidth
Produces the KV cache, then the first token every later token
Owns time to first token (TTFT) time per output token (TPOT)

stages.name: The path, hop by hop
stages.html:
Hop Does Adds to TTFT when
Gateway auth, per-tenant token limit, model routing limits are hit, or the route is cold
Queue / admission holds the request until a slot and KV memory are free the fleet is near capacity
Tokenize text to token IDs rarely, on very large prompts
Prefill one pass over the prompt, writes the KV cache the prompt is long, or the prefix cache misses
First decode step samples one token the batch is large
Stream out sends the token as an event a proxy buffers the response

Underneath, the scheduler runs continuous batching: the request joins a batch that is already in flight, between two decode steps.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
TTFT = queue wait + prefill time                              (all figures illustrative)
     = 50 ms + 2,000 prompt tokens / 5,000 tokens per second
     = 50 ms + 400 ms = 450 ms

end to end = TTFT + TPOT × (output tokens − 1)
           = 0.45 s + 0.025 s × 299 ≈ 7.9 s for a 300-token answer
Reading Consequence
the user waits 0.45 s to see something, 7.9 s for everything streaming changes what "latency" means
prefill time scales with prompt length a prompt ten times longer costs about ten times the prefill
with the stable prefix cached, only the new suffix is prefilled the 400 ms term can shrink to a small fraction

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Symptom Hop Cause
TTFT high for everyone, at once prefill another tenant's very long prompt holds the GPU
TTFT high in bursts queue admission waiting on KV memory
TTFT fine locally, poor in production stream out a load balancer or proxy buffers events
first request after idle is slow gateway, model cold replica, weights not loaded
TTFT rose after a prompt edit prefill the edit changed the prefix, so the cache stopped hitting

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: measure per stage, fix per stage
stages.html:
Spans to record:gatewayqueue waittokenizeprefillfirst decodefirst byte at the client
Term Lever Layer
queue wait admission control, priority tiers, more capacity scheduler, capacity
prefill prefix caching, shorter prompts, chunked prefill cache, prompt, scheduler
first byte disable buffering end to end, keep connections warm gateway

Why this matters: an SLO on TTFT only becomes actionable once it is split into these terms.

followUps.question: Why does prefill want different hardware behaviour from decode?
followUps.html:
Because one is limited by arithmetic and the other by reading memory.

Prefill Decode
Tokens per pass thousands one per sequence
Limited by matrix-multiply throughput reading weights and KV cache each step
Helped by more compute, attention kernels batching, smaller weights and cache

At scale some stacks run them on separate pools and hand the KV cache across.

followUps.question: "It's one forward pass, like any model endpoint."
followUps.html:
It is one pass for the prompt, then one pass per output token.

300-token answer = 1 prefill pass + 299 decode passes

That loop is why the request is long-lived, stateful and streamed.

followUps.question: The client disconnects after the first token.
followUps.html:
The server must notice and free the slot, or it keeps generating for nobody.

client closesgateway propagates cancelscheduler evicts the sequenceKV blocks freedslot reused

Without propagation, abandoned requests hold batch slots until max_tokens.

followUps.question: What is continuous batching doing while my request waits?
followUps.html:
Running other requests' decode steps, and admitting mine between two of them.

  • Per step the scheduler removes finished sequences and adds queued ones.
  • My prefill is slotted in, whole or in chunks.
  • No request waits for a whole batch to finish.

followUps.question: Which of these numbers goes in the SLO?
followUps.html:
TTFT and TPOT at p95 or p99, per workload tier.

Tier SLO on
interactive chat p95 TTFT, then a floor on tokens per second
agents, tools p95 end-to-end per step
batch completion deadline, no TTFT target

dontSay: "The model returns the response" — it returns a stream, one decode step at a time.
"Latency is 8 seconds" — which part: first token or last?
"Requests are batched together at the start" — they join and leave a running batch.

llm-serving-inference-q2.testing: whether you can explain why each phase has its bottleneck, and then pick a different optimisation for each.
llm-serving-inference-q2.trap: one latency number and one list of optimisations for both phases.
llm-serving-inference-q2.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Prefill is compute-bound and sets time to first token. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and sets time per output token."
2 · Why prefill is compute-bound "Prefill pushes the whole prompt through the network in one pass. Thousands of tokens share each read of the weights, so the GPU's arithmetic units are the limit."
3 · Why decode is bandwidth-bound "Decode processes one new token per sequence per step. To do that it still has to read every weight and that sequence's whole KV cache. The arithmetic is small; moving the bytes is the cost."
4 · Prove it "Roughly: thirty-five gigabytes of quantised weights on a GPU that can move about two thousand gigabytes a second gives at most about fifty-seven steps a second, however idle the compute is."
5 · So what for the system "So the levers differ. For prefill: attention kernels, prefix caching, chunking. For decode: batching, because one read of the weights then serves many sequences, plus smaller weights and a smaller cache. And capacity is about bandwidth and cache memory, not FLOPs."
Close "Prefill spends compute, decode spends bandwidth, and I optimise them as two separate problems."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
Prefill Decode
Tokens processed per pass the whole prompt one per sequence
Bottleneck compute (matrix multiplies, attention over n tokens) memory bandwidth (reading weights and KV cache)
Metric it owns TTFT TPOT
GPU looks busy under-used on compute, saturated on memory traffic

stages.name: Why prefill is compute-bound
stages.html:
One pass:read the weights onceapply them to n prompt tokens in parallelattention across all nKV cache for n tokens
  • The cost of loading the weights is shared by thousands of tokens, so the arithmetic dominates.
  • Attention over the prompt grows with the square of its length.
  • It is one burst of work; nothing is waiting on a previous step.

stages.name: Why decode is bandwidth-bound
stages.html:
One step:read all the weightsread this sequence's whole KV cachecompute for one tokenappend one K/V entryrepeat
What is read each step Size
model weights all of them, every step
KV cache grows by one token per step, per sequence
new computation one token's worth: tiny by comparison

The KV cache is what turned recomputation into memory: without it every step would redo the whole prompt.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
steps per second ≤ memory bandwidth / bytes read per step                (illustrative figures)
                 ≈ 2,000 GB/s / 35 GB of int4 weights  ≈ 57 steps per second

batch of 1   →  about 57 tokens per second
batch of 32  →  about 57 steps × 32 sequences, until the KV reads and compute start to matter
Reading Consequence
the ceiling is set by bytes, not FLOPs a "30% utilised" GPU can already be at its decode limit
each step serves the whole batch batching is nearly free throughput on decode
halving the weight bytes roughly doubles the ceiling quantisation makes decode faster, not just smaller

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Phase Levers Layer
Prefill prefix caching, shorter prompts, efficient attention kernels, chunked prefill cache, prompt, scheduler
Decode continuous batching, weight quantisation, GQA models, KV-cache quantisation, speculative decoding scheduler, model
Both separate pools for prefill-heavy and decode-heavy traffic at scale capacity

Architect's line: serving economics is bandwidth and cache real estate. FLOPs are the wrong unit for planning it.

followUps.question: Why does a bigger batch help decode at all?
followUps.html:
Because the weights are read once per step whatever the batch size.

Batch Weight reads per step Tokens out per step
1 1 1
32 1 32

The limit arrives when per-sequence KV reads and compute stop being small.

followUps.question: "GPU utilisation is 30%, so we have plenty of headroom."
followUps.html:
Utilisation reports compute activity, and decode is not limited by compute.

  • Memory bandwidth can be saturated at low reported utilisation.
  • KV-cache memory can be full with compute idle.
  • Capacity signals are queue depth, free KV blocks and SLO violations.

followUps.question: Is decode always bandwidth-bound?
followUps.html:
No. At large batch sizes compute fills up and the picture flips.

Regime Bound by
small batch bandwidth: compute is idle
large batch compute: every lane is busy

That flip is exactly when speculative decoding stops paying.

followUps.question: What is prefill/decode disaggregation?
followUps.html:
Running the two phases on separate pools and moving the KV cache between them.

requestprefill pooltransfer KV cachedecode poolstream

It removes interference between long prefills and running decodes, at the cost of the transfer and a more complex scheduler.

followUps.question: How does this change what hardware you buy?
followUps.html:
I'd size on memory capacity and bandwidth first, compute second.

Workload Dominant need
chat, long outputs bandwidth and VRAM for KV cache
long-prompt, short-answer (RAG, classification) compute for prefill
mixed measure the token mix before choosing

dontSay: "LLM inference is compute-bound" — only the prefill half.
"Utilisation is low, so we can take more traffic."
"Quantisation trades speed for memory" — on decode it buys both.

llm-serving-inference-q3.testing: whether you map each metric to its phase and can explain the batching trade in one sentence.
llm-serving-inference-q3.trap: quoting a mean latency for a streaming product.
llm-serving-inference-q3.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Time to first token is how long the user waits before anything appears. Time per output token is the gap between tokens after that. End to end is roughly the first plus the second times the output length."
2 · What drives TTFT "TTFT is queue wait plus prefill. It grows with prompt length, with scheduler pressure, and when a prefix cache misses."
3 · What drives TPOT "TPOT is the decode step time. It grows when more sequences share the batch, and when KV-cache pressure forces preemption."
4 · Where they trade "They trade through batching. A bigger batch gives more tokens per GPU-second, so cost per token falls. But requests wait longer to get in, which hurts TTFT, and each step is slower, which hurts TPOT. Individual levers also cut across: a long prefill stalls running decodes, and speculative decoding buys TPOT with extra compute."
5 · What I'd set as SLOs "So I set both at p95 or p99, per workload tier. Chat lives on TTFT and a readable token rate. Agents and batch jobs care about total completion. Then I pick the batch size that maximises goodput inside those limits."
Close "Two metrics, two phases, one dial between them, and the tier decides where the dial sits."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
TTFT       = queue wait + prefill time                     ← "does it start instantly"
TPOT       = time per decode step                          ← "does it flow"
end to end ≈ TTFT + TPOT × (output tokens − 1)             ← "when is it finished"
Metric Phase Felt by the user as
TTFT queue and prefill responsiveness
TPOT (or inter-token latency) decode reading speed
end to end both task completion

stages.name: What drives TTFT
stages.html:
Driver Effect Lever
prompt length prefill time grows with it shorter context, prefix caching
queue depth wait before a slot is free admission control, priority, capacity
prefix-cache miss the whole prompt is prefilled again stable prefix first, volatile content last
a neighbour's long prefill head-of-line blocking chunked prefill, a long-context pool
cold replica weights not loaded warm pool

stages.name: What drives TPOT
stages.html:
Driver Effect Lever
batch size each step serves more sequences and takes longer cap max batch per tier
weight and cache bytes more memory traffic per step quantisation, GQA models
KV pressure preemption and recompute pauses admission by KV occupancy
interleaved prefill chunks small pauses between steps tune the chunk size

stages.name: Where they trade
stages.html:
Lever Helps Hurts
larger batches cost per token TTFT (queueing) and TPOT (contention)
chunked prefill everyone else's TPOT the long prompt's own TTFT, slightly
speculative decoding TPOT compute headroom, so throughput at high load
prefix caching TTFT and cost nothing, if the prefix is stable

stages.name: What I'd set as SLOs
stages.html:
Tier Primary SLO Secondary Batch policy
interactive chat p95 TTFT minimum tokens per second small cap
agent steps p95 end to end per call — medium
bulk / offline completion deadline — as large as memory allows

Planning metric: goodput, the tokens per second from requests that met their SLO.

Why this matters: a mean hides the tail, and the tail is what users of a streaming product feel.

followUps.question: What token rate is "fast enough" for chat?
followUps.html:
Faster than people read; beyond that, users don't notice.

  • Reading speed is a few words per second, so a few tens of tokens per second already outruns it.
  • Past that point I'd spend capacity on TTFT or cost instead.
  • For agents nobody reads the stream, so total time is what counts.

followUps.question: "Average latency is 800 ms, we're within target."
followUps.html:
The average says nothing about the requests that hurt.

95 requests at 0.4 s and 5 between 2 and 4 s:   mean 0.52 s   p50 0.4 s   p99 4.0 s

One in a hundred users waits ten times longer, and a heavy user hits that tail many times a day.

followUps.question: 🧪 TTFT 0.6 s, TPOT 30 ms, 500 output tokens. End to end?
followUps.html:
About 15.6 seconds.

0.6 + 0.030 × 499 = 0.6 + 14.97 ≈ 15.6 s

So for long answers the output length, not TTFT, decides completion time.

followUps.question: Which metric does each cache improve?
followUps.html:
Prefix caching improves TTFT; an answer cache removes both.

Cache TTFT TPOT
prefix (KV) cache skips the cached part of prefill unchanged
semantic answer cache no model call at all no model call at all

followUps.question: Product asks for "instant and smooth". How do you turn that into numbers?
followUps.html:
Three targets, each with an owner and a lever.

Phrase Number Lever
"instant" p95 TTFT prefix cache, admission, chunked prefill
"smooth" p95 inter-token gap batch cap, quantisation
"affordable" goodput per GPU batch size inside the two limits above

dontSay: "Latency is X ms" — first token, per token, or total?
"Bigger batches are just more efficient" — they are, and they cost both latency metrics.
"We track the average."

llm-serving-inference-q4.testing: whether you can size concurrency from the KV-cache formula instead of from a utilisation graph.
llm-serving-inference-q4.trap: "GPU compute" or "it depends on the model" with no formula.
llm-serving-inference-q4.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Memory, not compute. Each in-flight request holds a KV cache that grows with its context length, and the GPU's memory left after the weights caps how many of those fit."
2 · How it works "The memory splits three ways: weights, which are fixed; the KV cache, which grows with traffic; and working activations. The cache costs two tensors per layer, times the number of KV heads, times head dimension, per token."
3 · Prove it "For a seventy-billion-class model with grouped-query attention that is about a third of a megabyte per token. With forty gigabytes free after quantised weights, about a hundred and twenty thousand tokens of cache fit: sixty requests at two thousand tokens, fifteen at eight thousand, three at thirty-two thousand, and not even one at a hundred and twenty-eight thousand."
4 · What it costs or breaks "So long contexts crowd out concurrency. One long session costs as much as many short ones, and when memory runs out the server preempts or rejects."
5 · So what for the system "That number is the capacity plan. I shrink the cache with a GQA model and cache quantisation, admit by free KV blocks, and price or tier long-context traffic separately."
Close "Weights are a fixed cost; the KV cache is the variable one, and it sets concurrency."

stages.name: The one-line claim
How it works
stages.html:
KV bytes per token = 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_value
                     └ K and V ┘
70B-class with GQA:  2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 (fp16) = 327,680 bytes ≈ 0.33 MB per token

concurrency ≈ (VRAM − weights − overhead) / (KV bytes per token × average context)
Term Set by Can I change it at serving time?
layers, head_dim the model no
kv_heads MHA, GQA or MQA, fixed at pre-training no: choose the model
bytes per value cache precision yes: KV-cache quantisation
context length the traffic yes: limits, trimming, tiers

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Prove it — one 80 GB GPU, int4 weights:

per_token = 2 * 80 * 8 * 128 * 2            # layers, KV heads, head_dim, fp16 bytes: a 70B-class GQA model
free = (80 - 35 - 5) * 1e9                     # one 80 GB GPU, int4 weights 35 GB, 5 GB overhead (illustrative)
budget = free / per_token                      # tokens of KV cache that fit
print(per_token, "bytes per token |", round(budget), "cached tokens fit")
for ctx in (2_000, 8_000, 32_000, 128_000):
    print(ctx, "token contexts →", int(budget // ctx), "concurrent")
# → 327680 bytes per token | 122070 cached tokens fit
# → 2000 token contexts → 61 concurrent
# → 8000 token contexts → 15 concurrent
# → 32000 token contexts → 3 concurrent
# → 128000 token contexts → 0 concurrent
Context per request Concurrent requests
2,000 tokens 61
8,000 tokens 15
32,000 tokens 3
128,000 tokens 0: one such session doesn't fit on this GPU

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
When KV memory runs out What the server does What users see
admission waits new requests queue TTFT rises
preemption a running sequence is evicted, later recomputed a pause mid-stream
rejection the request is refused an error
nothing is controlled out-of-memory the replica restarts

Example: a single tenant sending 32k-token prompts uses the memory of sixteen ordinary 2k-token chats per request.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: plan and admit by KV memory
stages.html:
Lever Effect on the formula Layer
GQA or MQA model fewer KV heads model choice
KV-cache quantisation fewer bytes per value model, scheduler
paged allocation no worst-case reservation, less waste scheduler
context limits and trimming per tier smaller average context gateway, prompt
long-context pool isolates the expensive requests capacity
prefix sharing shared blocks counted once cache

Signals to scale and admit on: free KV blocks, queue depth, TTFT violations. Not GPU utilisation.

followUps.question: Why is the cache there at all?
followUps.html:
To avoid recomputing keys and values for every earlier token at every step.

Without cache:each step re-runs the whole sequencequadratic work
With cache:each step computes one token and reads the restlinear work, paid for in memory

followUps.question: "We're at 40% GPU utilisation, so we can double traffic."
followUps.html:
Not if the KV cache is already full.

  • Utilisation measures compute activity.
  • Concurrency is capped by memory.
  • Check free KV blocks and admission wait before promising headroom.

followUps.question: 🧪 Same GPU, MHA instead of GQA: how many 8k-token requests fit?
followUps.html:
One.

MHA has 64 KV heads instead of 8  →  8× the cache: 2.62 MB per token
8,000 tokens × 2.62 MB ≈ 21 GB per request   →   40 GB free / 21 GB = 1 request

followUps.question: What does PagedAttention change here?
followUps.html:
It allocates the cache in small blocks on demand instead of reserving the maximum length per request.

Allocation Memory held by a 500-token request with an 8k limit
contiguous, worst case 8k tokens' worth
paged about 500 tokens' worth

The formula's ceiling is the same; paging lets you reach it.

followUps.question: How do you charge tenants fairly given this?
followUps.html:
By tokens and by how long they hold cache memory, not by request.

Unit Captures
input and output tokens compute and bandwidth used
context length tier KV memory reserved
priority class the right to preempt others

A flat per-request price makes the 32k-token tenant everyone else's cost.

dontSay: "Compute limits concurrency."
"It depends on the model" — say on which four terms.
"Capacity is fine, utilisation is low."

llm-serving-inference-q5.testing: whether you can name the specific waste each one removed: idle slots, and reserved-but-unused memory.
llm-serving-inference-q5.trap: calling them model optimisations. Neither touches the model.
llm-serving-inference-q5.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Each fixed a different waste. Continuous batching fixed a scheduling waste: GPU slots sitting idle. PagedAttention fixed a memory waste: cache space reserved and never used."
2 · How continuous batching works "Static batching ran a batch until its longest sequence finished, so short answers left empty slots. Continuous batching schedules per decode step: a finished sequence leaves, a queued one joins at once."
3 · How paging works "The KV cache used to be one contiguous block per request, sized for the maximum length. Most requests never reach it, so memory was stranded and fragmented. PagedAttention stores the cache in small fixed-size blocks with a lookup table, like virtual memory, and allocates as tokens arrive."
4 · Prove it "A small simulation: twelve requests on four slots take six hundred and thirty steps with static batching at forty-eight percent slot use, and four hundred and thirty-five steps with continuous batching at seventy percent."
5 · So what for the system "Together they give more tokens per second and more concurrent requests on the same hardware with the same model. It is the standard case that LLM serving is a systems problem."
Close "One refills slots every step, the other stops reserving memory for tokens that never come."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: a scheduling waste and a memory waste
stages.html:
Continuous batching PagedAttention
Waste removed batch slots idle after short sequences finish KV memory reserved for the maximum length
Mechanism admit and evict every decode step fixed-size blocks plus an indirection table
Kind of work scheduler memory allocator
Result higher slot use, lower queue wait larger effective batch, less fragmentation

stages.name: How continuous batching works
stages.html:
Static:form a batchrun until the longest finishesreturn allform the next
Continuous:each decode stepremove finished sequencesadmit queued onesnext step
Problem with static batching Effect
waits for the longest sequence finished slots idle; their users also wait if results are returned together
the batch must be formed first arriving requests queue for a whole batch duration
prompts padded to the longest memory and compute spent on padding

stages.name: How paging works
stages.html:
Contiguous:reserve max-length space per requestmost of it unusedfew requests fit
Paged:allocate a block when tokens need ittable maps logical to physical blocksfree blocks reused by anyone
Gain Why
no worst-case reservation memory tracks the tokens that exist
almost no fragmentation all blocks are the same size
prefix sharing two requests with the same system prompt point at the same physical blocks
cheap preemption blocks are freed and reallocated without moving data

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: the same twelve requests, two schedulers
stages.html:
Prove it — output lengths differ by ten times, four batch slots:

lengths = [20, 200, 30, 180, 25, 190, 40, 210, 35, 15, 220, 45]     # output tokens per request
B = 4                                                              # batch slots
static = sum(max(lengths[i:i + B]) for i in range(0, len(lengths), B))   # each batch runs until its longest ends
slots = [0] * B                                                    # continuous: a freed slot is refilled at once
for n in lengths:
    i = slots.index(min(slots)); slots[i] += n
continuous = max(slots)
useful = sum(lengths)
print("static:", static, "steps, slot use", round(useful / (static * B), 2))
print("continuous:", continuous, "steps, slot use", round(useful / (continuous * B), 2))
# → static: 630 steps, slot use 0.48
# → continuous: 435 steps, slot use 0.7
Scheduler Decode steps to finish all Share of slot-steps doing useful work
static 630 0.48
continuous 435 0.70

A simplified model: real schedulers also bound the batch by KV memory, which is where paging comes in.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
What you get From
more tokens per second per GPU slots refilled every step
more concurrent requests memory no longer stranded
lower queue wait no waiting for a batch to form
prefix caching that pays more shared blocks
What to tune Trade
maximum batch size throughput against TPOT
prefill chunk size a long prompt's TTFT against everyone else's TPOT

Fix layer: scheduler and allocator. This is what an inference server such as vLLM or TGI provides over a bare model loop.

followUps.question: What happens to a new request's prefill under continuous batching?
followUps.html:
It is slotted between decode steps, whole or in chunks.

Policy Effect
whole prefill at once running streams pause for its full length
chunked prefill short pauses, spread out

followUps.question: "These are model optimisations, like quantisation."
followUps.html:
Neither changes a weight or an output.

  • Continuous batching changes when sequences run.
  • Paging changes where the cache lives.
  • The tokens produced are identical.

followUps.question: All requests have the same output length. Does continuous batching still help?
followUps.html:
Much less: its gain comes from variance in length.

Workload Gain
uniform lengths, arriving together (offline batch) small
mixed lengths, arriving at random (chat) large

Paging still helps wherever requests are shorter than the reserved maximum.

followUps.question: How would you justify adopting such a server to an infra team?
followUps.html:
Same GPUs, same model, measurably more goodput.

  • Run both on recorded traffic with the same SLO.
  • Compare goodput, p95 TTFT and peak concurrent requests.
  • No retraining, no quality evaluation needed, because outputs don't change.

followUps.question: What new operational risks come with it?
followUps.html:
Requests now interfere with each other inside one batch.

Risk Control
a long prefill stalls others chunked prefill, token limits per tier
shared prefix blocks across tenants scope prefix sharing per tenant
preemption under memory pressure admission by free blocks, priority classes

dontSay: "Continuous batching makes the model faster" — it makes the GPU less idle.
"PagedAttention is a new attention mechanism" — it is a memory allocator.
"Batching means waiting for a batch to fill."

llm-serving-inference-q6.testing: whether you know the cache matches on an exact token prefix, and can design a prompt so it keeps hitting.
llm-serving-inference-q6.trap: confusing it with a semantic answer cache, or putting a timestamp at the top of the system prompt.
llm-serving-inference-q6.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Prefix caching reuses the KV cache for a prompt prefix the server has already processed, so that part of prefill is skipped. It cuts time to first token and cost on every request that shares the prefix."
2 · How it works "The match is on exact tokens from the first position onward. The cached part ends at the first token that differs; everything after that is computed as usual."
3 · Prove it "With three hundred stable system tokens first and the timestamp after them, three hundred and one of three hundred and four tokens are reused. Put the timestamp first, and one token is reused."
4 · Where it silently breaks "That is how it fails without an error: a date or a user name at the top, tools listed in a different order, a prompt edit, whitespace changes, or the entry expiring. The request still works; it is just slower and costlier."
5 · So what for the system "So I order prompts stable to volatile: system text, tool definitions, examples, then history, then the new input. And I track the cached-token share per route, with an alert when it drops."
Close "Exact prefix, stable content first, and a metric that tells me when it stopped."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: skip the prefill you already did
stages.html:
Prefix (KV) cache Semantic answer cache
Stores KV tensors for a token prefix a finished answer
Matches on exact tokens from position 0 embedding similarity of the question
Saves part of prefill the whole model call
Risk none for correctness a stale or wrong answer for a near-match

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: match up to the first difference
stages.html:
Request:tokenizefind the longest cached prefixreuse its KV blocksprefill only the remaining suffixdecode
Good candidates for the cached prefix Why
system prompt identical on every request
tool and schema definitions long and stable
few-shot examples long and stable
conversation so far each turn extends the previous prefix
agent scratchpad each step appends to the last

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Prove it — shared prefix length between two consecutive requests:

def shared(a, b):
    n = 0
    for x, y in zip(a, b):
        if x != y: break
        n += 1
    return n
system = ["sys"] * 300                                             # 300 stable system-prompt tokens
good = [system + ["time", t, "user", u] for t, u in (("10:01", "hi"), ("10:02", "hello"))]
bad = [ ["time", t] + system + ["user", u] for t, u in (("10:01", "hi"), ("10:02", "hello"))]
print("volatile last: ", shared(*good), "of", len(good[1]), "tokens reused")
print("volatile first:", shared(*bad), "of", len(bad[1]), "tokens reused")
# → volatile last:  301 of 304 tokens reused
# → volatile first: 1 of 304 tokens reused
Layout Tokens reused Prefill still needed
stable first, volatile last 301 of 304 3 tokens
volatile first 1 of 304 303 tokens

Same content, same total length; only the position of the timestamp changed.

stages.name: Where it silently breaks
stages.html:
Cause Why the cache misses
timestamp, request ID or user name in the system prompt the prefix differs on every request
tools or examples serialised in a different order same content, different tokens
a prompt edit or template version change everything after the edit is new
whitespace or formatting differences different tokens
entry expired or evicted caches are time- and memory-bounded
request routed to another replica a local cache lives on one machine
model or tokenizer changed the cached tensors are for another model

Why "silently": the response is correct either way. Only TTFT and cost move.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Prompt order:system texttool definitionsexamplesretrieved contextconversationvolatile values and the new input
Practice Layer
deterministic serialisation of tools and JSON (fixed key order) prompt
volatile values at the end, or passed as a late message prompt
route a session to the replica that holds its cache gateway
cached-token share per route as a metric, with an alert observability
prompt changes reviewed for their effect on the prefix release process

followUps.question: How do hosted APIs expose this?
followUps.html:
As automatic or opt-in prompt caching, with cached tokens reported in the usage data.

  • Read the usage fields to see how many input tokens were served from cache.
  • Entries expire after a short idle period, so low-traffic routes hit less often.
  • Details differ by provider and change; check the current documentation.

followUps.question: "We added a semantic cache, so we have prefix caching covered."
followUps.html:
They are different caches for different savings.

Request Prefix cache Semantic cache
new question, same system prompt hit miss
repeated question hit hit: no model call

Most systems want both, with the semantic one guarded for staleness.

followUps.question: Is a shared prefix cache safe across tenants?
followUps.html:
Treat it as a possible side channel.

Risk Control
a fast response reveals that someone else sent the same prefix scope the cache per tenant
shared boilerplate only allow cross-tenant sharing for public, identical system text

followUps.question: Does retrieved context help or hurt the hit rate?
followUps.html:
It ends the shared prefix wherever it is inserted.

Hurts:systemretrieved chunkslong instructions (instructions are never cached)
Better:systemlong instructionsretrieved chunksquestion

followUps.question: The bill doubled with flat traffic. Could this be it?
followUps.html:
It is one of the first three things I'd check.

Check Finding that confirms it
cached-token share per route, over time a step down on a deploy date
the prompt diff on that date a change near the top
TTFT on the same route rose at the same moment

dontSay: "Prefix caching caches the answer" — it caches the work of reading the prompt.
"It matches similar prompts" — it matches identical token prefixes.
"It's a provider feature, nothing to design" — prompt order decides whether it ever fires.

llm-serving-inference-q7.testing: whether you know the failure modes that exist only because the response is a long-lived stream: buffering, mid-stream errors, cancellation.
llm-serving-inference-q7.trap: "we use SSE", with nothing about proxies, errors after the 200, or freeing the GPU slot.
llm-serving-inference-q7.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Streaming sends each token to the client as it is decoded, so the user's perceived latency becomes the time to first token and not the total."
2 · How it works "The server holds the HTTP response open and writes one event per decode step, usually as server-sent events. The client appends each piece as it arrives. A final event marks the end and carries the usage counts."
3 · Prove it "One detail shows the care needed. Tokens are byte pieces, so a chunk can end in the middle of a character. Decoding each chunk naively raises an error; an incremental decoder holds the partial bytes until the character is complete."
4 · What breaks it "In production it breaks in four places. A proxy or load balancer buffers the response, so tokens arrive in one lump. An idle timeout cuts a slow stream. An error happens after the status code was already sent as two hundred. And the client leaves, but the server keeps generating."
5 · So what for the system "So I disable buffering on every hop, send heartbeats, define an in-band error event, and make cancellation propagate to the scheduler so the GPU slot and its cache are freed."
Close "The stream is the product: it has to survive the network path, fail in a way the client can read, and stop when the user does."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
Non-streaming Streaming
User sees first text after the whole generation TTFT
Connection short request, one response held open for the whole generation
Errors a status code may occur after the status was sent
Server state none after the response a GPU slot and KV cache for the stream's lifetime

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
Transport Fits
Server-sent events one-way token streams over plain HTTP: the common default
WebSocket two-way sessions: voice, interruptions, tool traffic in both directions

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Prove it — the bytes of "café 👍 ok" split into 4-byte chunks:

import codecs
data = "caf\u00e9 \U0001F44D ok".encode()               # "café 👍 ok" as UTF-8 bytes
chunks = [data[i:i + 4] for i in range(0, len(data), 4)]
try:
    print([c.decode() for c in chunks])
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    print("naive flush:", e.reason)
dec = codecs.getincrementaldecoder("utf-8")()
print("buffered:", [dec.decode(c) for c in chunks])
# → naive flush: unexpected end of data
# → buffered: ['caf', 'é ', '👍 o', 'k']
Approach Result
decode each chunk by itself fails: a chunk ends inside a multi-byte character
incremental decoder holds the partial bytes and emits whole characters only

The same care applies to streamed JSON and tool arguments: parse incrementally, or wait for the closing event.

stages.name: What breaks it
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Cause Fix, and its layer
Buffering fine locally; in production the answer arrives all at once a proxy, load balancer or compression layer collects the body disable response buffering and compression for the stream (gateway)
Idle timeout long or slow streams are cut an intermediary closes "idle" connections heartbeat comments; raise timeouts (gateway)
Mid-stream error the client shows a truncated answer as if complete the 200 was sent before the failure an in-band error event, and a finish_reason on every stream (API contract)
Zombie generation GPU busy, nobody listening disconnect is not propagated cancel on disconnect, free the slot and the KV blocks (scheduler)
No backpressure server memory grows a slow client, an unbounded write buffer bounded buffers; drop or pause (server)

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Stream lifecycle:openfirst tokentokensexactly one terminal event: done, error or cancelled
Contract item Why
every stream ends with a terminal event the client can tell complete from cut off
errors are events with a type retryable or not is machine-readable
usage is reported at the end billing and budgets for partial output
retries are safe an idempotency key, so a reconnect doesn't bill or act twice

Metrics: TTFT at the client, not the server, plus stream abort rate and time to release a slot after disconnect.

followUps.question: SSE or WebSocket?
followUps.html:
SSE unless the client must talk during the stream.

Need Choose
tokens down, nothing up SSE: plain HTTP, simple through proxies
interruptions, audio, two-way tool traffic WebSocket

followUps.question: "TTFT is 300 ms on my machine, so streaming works."
followUps.html:
Measure it where the user is.

Local:serverclient: events arrive one by one
Production:serverload balancerCDNclient: any hop may buffer

A single buffering hop turns a stream back into a slow non-streaming response.

followUps.question: The model fails after 200 tokens. What does the client get?
followUps.html:
An error event, and the partial text marked as incomplete.

  • The status code can't change; it was sent with the first byte.
  • The UI shows what arrived, flagged as interrupted, with a retry.
  • For structured output the partial JSON is discarded, not parsed.

followUps.question: How do you stream structured output or tool calls?
followUps.html:
Stream the deltas, act only on the completed object.

argument fragments arriveaccumulateterminal eventvalidate against the schemathen execute

Executing on a half-received tool call is a correctness bug.

followUps.question: What does an abandoned stream cost?
followUps.html:
A batch slot and KV memory until max_tokens, unless cancellation works.

Without cancellation With it
slot held for the full generation slot freed within one decode step
output tokens produced for nobody generation stops

On a busy fleet that is real capacity, so I'd track tokens generated after disconnect as a waste metric.

dontSay: "We just use SSE" — the transport is the easy part.
"Errors return a 500" — not after the stream started.
"Closing the socket stops the request" — only if the server propagates it.

llm-serving-inference-q8.testing: whether you can define a single metric that can't be gamed by trading away the SLO.
llm-serving-inference-q8.trap: reporting tokens per second with no SLO attached.
llm-serving-inference-q8.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Throughput is tokens per second per GPU: the cost side. Latency is what each user feels. They pull against each other through batch size."
2 · Why throughput misleads "Throughput alone is easy to inflate. Push the batch to sixty-four and tokens per second look great, while most requests miss their time-to-first-token target."
3 · Why latency misleads "Latency alone is just as easy: run every request alone on a GPU and it is superb, and the cost per token is absurd."
4 · What goodput measures "Goodput counts only the tokens from requests that met their SLO. In a small example the large batch has two thousand four hundred tokens a second of throughput but only four hundred and eighty of goodput, because eighty percent of its requests were late. The small batch delivers nine hundred, all on time."
5 · How I'd tune to it "So I fix the SLO per workload tier, then raise the batch and the load until goodput stops rising. That knee is the operating point, and it is the number I use for capacity planning."
Close "Goodput is throughput that the user would actually accept."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Metric Answers Gamed by
throughput (tokens/s per GPU) how cheap is a token huge batches
latency (TTFT, TPOT at p95) how good is the experience tiny batches, idle GPUs
goodput how many useful tokens per GPU-second neither

stages.name: Why throughput misleads
stages.html:
The trick:raise max batchmore sequences per steptokens per second upqueue wait and step time upSLO missed
  • A benchmark that reports only tokens per second rewards exactly this.
  • A late token in a chat product has little value: the user has already left or retried.

stages.name: Why latency misleads
stages.html:
Configuration p95 TTFT Cost per token
one request per GPU excellent many times higher
batch tuned to the SLO within target reasonable

Beating the SLO by a wide margin is capacity paid for and not used.

stages.name: What goodput measures
stages.claim: only tokens that met the SLO
stages.html:
goodput = tokens per second from requests that met every SLO (TTFT, TPOT, deadline)

Prove it — two batch settings against a 0.5 s TTFT SLO (illustrative samples):

slo = 0.5                                       # TTFT SLO in seconds
runs = {"max batch 8": (900, [.2, .25, .3, .3, .35, .4, .4, .45, .45, .48]),
        "max batch 64": (2400, [.3, .5, .6, .7, .8, .9, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0])}     # tokens/s, sampled TTFTs (illustrative)
for name, (tps, ttft) in runs.items():
    ok = sum(t <= slo for t in ttft) / len(ttft)
    print(name, "| throughput", tps, "| in SLO", ok, "| goodput", round(tps * ok))
# → max batch 8 | throughput 900 | in SLO 1.0 | goodput 900
# → max batch 64 | throughput 2400 | in SLO 0.2 | goodput 480
Setting Throughput Requests in SLO Goodput
max batch 8 900 100% 900
max batch 64 2,400 20% 480

The configuration with 2.7 times the throughput delivers about half the goodput.

stages.name: How I'd tune to it
stages.html:
Procedure:fix the SLO per tierreplay realistic trafficraise load and max batchrecord goodputoperate just below the knee
Use Metric
capacity planning goodput per GPU at the tier's SLO
finance cost per token, derived from goodput
comparing servers or settings goodput on the same traffic and SLO

followUps.question: Which levers move the knee to the right?
followUps.html:
Anything that removes interference between requests.

  • Chunked prefill: long prompts stop stalling decodes.
  • Tier separation: chat and batch get different batch caps.
  • Admission control: shed or queue before the SLO is lost for everyone.
  • Prefix caching: less prefill work per request.

followUps.question: "Our server does 5,000 tokens per second."
followUps.html:
At what SLO, on what traffic?

Missing detail Why it matters
SLO without it the number may be all late tokens
prompt and output length mix prefill-heavy and decode-heavy loads differ
arrival pattern bursty traffic queues more than steady traffic

followUps.question: A batch workload has no latency SLO. Is goodput meaningless?
followUps.html:
Its SLO is a deadline, so goodput becomes throughput that finishes in time.

Tier SLO in the goodput definition
chat TTFT and TPOT
batch job completed before its deadline

For batch that usually means: maximise raw throughput.

followUps.question: How do you measure it in production?
followUps.html:
From per-request traces.

each requestrecord TTFT, TPOT, tokens, tiermark "met SLO"sum tokens of the ones that did, per GPU-second

followUps.question: How does goodput enter a capacity plan?
followUps.html:
It converts a traffic forecast into a GPU count.

GPUs needed = peak tokens per second demanded (per tier) / goodput per GPU at that tier's SLO  + headroom

Planning from raw throughput under-provisions, because it assumes a batch size the SLO forbids.

dontSay: "We maximise throughput" — at whose latency?
"Lower latency is always better" — past the SLO it is wasted capacity.
A tokens-per-second number with no SLO, traffic mix or percentile.

llm-serving-inference-q9.testing: whether "no visible quality drop" becomes an evaluation gate you define, and whether you know what quantisation buys beyond memory.
llm-serving-inference-q9.trap: "4-bit is fine, the paper shows less than one percent loss."
llm-serving-inference-q9.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "First I'd ask what 'visible' means here: which tasks, which languages, and who judges. And what hardware is the target, because that sets how low I must go."
2 · Constraints and numbers "Seventy billion parameters are a hundred and forty gigabytes in sixteen-bit, seventy in eight-bit and thirty-five in four-bit. So four-bit fits one eighty-gigabyte GPU with room for the KV cache; eight-bit needs two."
3 · Baseline plan "I'd start with weight-only quantisation, eight-bit first and then four-bit, using a calibrated method. Weights are static, so this is the low-risk step. And because decode is limited by memory bandwidth, smaller weights are also faster."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The hard part is proving quality held. I'd run my own task evaluation against the full-precision model, by dimension: reasoning, long outputs, code, non-English, format compliance. Perplexity alone misses task regressions. I ship the lowest precision that passes every gate."
5 · Failure modes "Regressions hide in the tails: long context, arithmetic, rare languages. And the speed-up only appears if the kernels for that format are good on my hardware."
6 · Evolve "I keep the unquantised model routable for a one-flag rollback, then consider KV-cache quantisation for more concurrency."
Close "Weight-only first, my evaluation as the gate, and a rollback path that stays open."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
Ask Why
which tasks and languages matter? degradation is uneven across them
who or what judges quality? an eval set, side-by-side review, or live metrics
what hardware, how many GPUs? sets the target size
latency and concurrency targets? decides whether the KV cache also needs shrinking

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
weights = parameters × bytes per parameter
70 × 10⁹ × 2 bytes   (fp16)  = 140 GB   → 2 × 80 GB GPUs, almost nothing left for KV cache
70 × 10⁹ × 1 byte    (int8)  =  70 GB   → 2 GPUs comfortably, or 1 with a few GB for cache
70 × 10⁹ × 0.5 byte  (int4)  =  35 GB   → 1 GPU, about 40 GB left for KV cache
Precision Typical quality Memory Decode speed
fp16 reference 1× reference
8-bit weights usually indistinguishable 0.5× faster
4-bit weights task-dependent; large models hold up better 0.25× faster again

Real files run a little larger than these figures: some layers stay at higher precision.

stages.name: Baseline plan
stages.html:
Rungs:fp16 baseline8-bit weightsevaluate4-bit weights with a calibrated methodevaluateship the lowest that passes
Choice Reason
weights before activations static, calibratable once, no runtime outliers
calibrated methods (GPTQ- or AWQ-class) they protect the weights that matter most
calibration data from my own domain the method optimises for what it sees
win is memory and bandwidth exactly what decode is bound by

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.html:
Dimension fp16 8-bit 4-bit Gate
core task quality measure measure measure within the agreed margin
reasoning and multi-step measure measure measure within margin
long-form coherence, long context measure measure measure within margin
code and arithmetic measure measure measure within margin
non-English measure measure measure within margin
format and schema compliance measure measure measure no drop
blind side-by-side preference — measure measure no significant preference for fp16
Order:offline evalside-by-side on sampled real promptsshadow trafficcanaryfull rollout

Why not perplexity alone: it averages over tokens and under-detects failures in the specific behaviours above.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Tail regressions averages fine; long reasoning chains or rare languages worse sliced evals, not one score
No speed-up smaller model, same latency check kernel support for that format on that GPU
Calibration mismatch good on benchmarks, worse on domain text calibrate on in-domain samples
Stacked changes quantised and re-prompted at once change one thing per release
Silent drift after rollout complaints weeks later keep the eval running on production samples

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Next step Why
keep fp16 or 8-bit routable rollback is a routing flag, not a redeploy
route hard requests to the higher precision quality where it is needed, savings elsewhere
KV-cache quantisation more concurrent requests and longer contexts
adapters on the quantised base tenant customisation without more full copies

followUps.question: Why is the quantised model faster, not just smaller?
followUps.html:
Because each decode step reads all the weights, and there are fewer bytes to read.

decode steps per second ≤ memory bandwidth / weight bytes        ← halve the bytes, roughly double the ceiling

followUps.question: "The paper reports under 1% loss at 4-bit."
followUps.html:
On their benchmarks, as an average.

Their number My question
average over public tasks what about my task and my languages
one model family does it hold for mine
perplexity or accuracy does format compliance survive

The paper tells me it is worth trying; my evaluation tells me whether to ship.

followUps.question: The hardware holds only half the fp16 weights. What breaks first at lower bits?
followUps.html:
Small models and very low bit-widths degrade first.

Situation Expectation
4-bit on a large model usually holds
4-bit on a small model more visible loss
below 4-bit sharp, task-dependent drops

A larger model at 4-bit often beats a smaller model at fp16 in the same memory. That is a comparison to measure, not assume.

followUps.question: How does this interact with fine-tuning?
followUps.html:
Train low-rank adapters on top of the frozen quantised base.

quantise the basefreeze ittrain LoRA adapters (the QLoRA pattern)serve base plus adapters

followUps.question: How do you present the decision?
followUps.html:
As cost saved against quality risk, with the rollback stated.

Option GPUs per replica Eval result Rollback
fp16 2 reference —
8-bit 1–2 measure route flag
4-bit 1 measure route flag

dontSay: "4-bit is basically lossless."
"We checked perplexity."
"Quantisation trades speed for size" — on decode it gains both.

llm-serving-inference-q10.testing: whether you connect the choice to the decode bottleneck and to the outlier problem in activations.
llm-serving-inference-q10.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "There are three things to quantise: weights, activations and the KV cache. They differ in how hard they are and in which bottleneck they relieve."
2 · Where weight-only wins "Weight-only wins for LLM serving because decode is limited by memory bandwidth, and the weights are the bytes read every step. They are also static, so I can calibrate them once offline."
3 · Where activations pay "Activations are computed at run time and a few channels carry very large values. A small example: with one outlier, four-bit quantisation maps every normal value to the same level. So activation quantisation needs per-channel scales and outlier handling. What it buys is cheaper arithmetic, which helps the compute-bound prefill and integer-only hardware."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask which phase dominates my cost, and what my hardware runs fast. Kernel support decides as much as theory."
5 · What I'd pick here "For a GPU-served chat model: weight-only first, then KV-cache quantisation for concurrency, and activation quantisation only when prefill dominates or the target is an edge accelerator."
Close "Shrink what the bottleneck reads, which is the weights, and leave the hard part until it pays."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Weights Activations KV cache
Known when offline, fixed at run time, per input at run time, per request
Difficulty low: calibrate once high: outlier channels medium
Relieves memory, and bandwidth in decode compute in prefill memory per request: concurrency
Notation W4A16, W8A16 W8A8 separate setting

stages.name: Where weight-only wins
stages.html:
Each decode step:read all weightsread this sequence's KV cachea little arithmeticone token
Reason Detail
matches the bottleneck fewer weight bytes per step means more steps per second
static no surprises at run time
mature tooling calibrated methods and fast kernels are widely available
activations stay fp16 the outlier problem is avoided entirely

stages.name: Where activations pay
stages.html:
Prove it — uniform quantisation of six values, one of them an outlier:

w = [0.02, -0.01, 0.03, -0.02, 0.01, 4.0]        # five normal values and one outlier
def quant(xs, bits):
    lo, hi = min(xs), max(xs); step = (hi - lo) / (2 ** bits - 1)
    return [round(lo + round((x - lo) / step) * step, 3) for x in xs]
print("8-bit, with outlier:", quant(w, 8))
print("4-bit, with outlier:", quant(w, 4))
print("4-bit, outlier apart:", quant(w[:-1], 4))
# → 8-bit, with outlier: [0.027, -0.004, 0.027, -0.02, 0.012, 4.0]
# → 4-bit, with outlier: [-0.02, -0.02, -0.02, -0.02, -0.02, 4.0]
# → 4-bit, outlier apart: [0.02, -0.01, 0.03, -0.02, 0.01]
Case What happens to the five normal values
8-bit, outlier in range coarse but distinct
4-bit, outlier in range all collapse to one level: the information is gone
4-bit, outlier handled separately preserved exactly
Activation quantisation needs Because
per-channel scales channels differ by orders of magnitude
outlier-aware schemes a few values would otherwise set the range
calibration on representative inputs ranges depend on the data

What it buys: integer arithmetic. That matters for compute-bound prefill, and for CPUs and edge accelerators.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
If Then
decode dominates (chat, long outputs) on GPUs weight-only
memory per request limits concurrency add KV-cache quantisation
prefill dominates (long prompts, short answers) activation quantisation starts to pay
target is a phone, CPU or integer-only accelerator W8A8 or lower is often required
the hardware lacks fast kernels for the format no speed-up, whatever the theory says

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.html:
Order:W8A16W4A16KV-cache quantisationactivations, only with a measured reason
Step Gate before the next
weight-only task evaluation against fp16
KV cache long-context and long-conversation slices
activations per-channel calibration, and a benchmark that shows real speed-up on my hardware

followUps.question: What do GPTQ- and AWQ-class methods actually do?
followUps.html:
They choose quantised weights that preserve layer outputs on calibration data, instead of rounding each weight alone.

Idea Effect
compensate rounding error across weights the layer's output changes less
weight by activation magnitude weights that matter most keep more precision

followUps.question: "Lower bits everywhere means faster everywhere."
followUps.html:
Only where the kernels exist and the bottleneck is the thing you shrank.

  • No fast kernel: the format is unpacked to fp16 at run time, with no gain.
  • Wrong bottleneck: cheaper arithmetic doesn't help a bandwidth-bound step.
  • Quality: each extra tensor quantised adds risk.

followUps.question: Where do FP8 formats fit?
followUps.html:
As a floating-point middle ground that newer GPUs support natively.

Format Character
int8 uniform steps: struggles with wide ranges
fp8 floating point: handles ranges better, needs hardware support

Whether it beats int8 for a given model is measured, not assumed.

followUps.question: Why does KV-cache quantisation deserve its own decision?
followUps.html:
Because it targets a different limit: memory per request.

KV bytes per token = 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_value     ← halve the last term, double the concurrency

Its risk shows up in long contexts, so that slice is the gate.

followUps.question: Who should own this decision?
followUps.html:
The serving team proposes; the evaluation gate decides.

Input Owner
memory and latency gain serving
quality by slice whoever owns the product's eval set
rollback path serving, agreed before rollout

dontSay: "Quantise everything to 4-bit."
"Activations are just like weights" — they have run-time outliers.
"It's a pure speed-memory trade" — hardware support decides whether there is any speed.

llm-serving-inference-q11.testing: whether you can explain the speed-up from the bandwidth-bound nature of decode, state that the output distribution is unchanged, and say when it stops paying.
llm-serving-inference-q11.trap: calling it an approximation, or enabling it for every tier.
llm-serving-inference-q11.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "It is faster because decode at small batch is limited by memory bandwidth, so the GPU has spare compute. Speculative decoding spends that spare compute to take fewer sequential steps of the large model."
2 · How it works "A small draft model proposes a few tokens. The large model then scores all of them in one parallel pass, which costs about the same as generating one token. It accepts the longest prefix that passes an acceptance test, and resamples at the first rejection."
3 · Prove it "The test accepts a token with probability the minimum of one and target over draft probability, which makes the output distributed exactly as the large model's. With eighty percent acceptance and four drafted tokens, each large-model pass yields about three point four tokens instead of one."
4 · When it breaks "It breaks in two ways. If acceptance is low, from a mismatched draft, unusual text or high temperature, the drafts are wasted. And if the GPU is already compute-saturated by a large batch, there is no spare compute to spend, so it costs throughput."
5 · So what for the system "So it is a latency tool. I enable it for the interactive tier at small batch, measure acceptance rate per route, and leave it off for the throughput tier."
Close "More FLOPs, fewer serial steps, the same distribution, and only while compute is idle."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: spend idle compute to skip serial steps
stages.html:
Resource at small batch State Speculative decoding
memory bandwidth saturated: every step reads all weights fewer large-model steps
compute mostly idle used to verify several tokens per step

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: draft, verify in one pass, accept a prefix
stages.html:
Variant Draft comes from
separate draft model a smaller model with the same tokenizer
self-speculation (Medusa-, EAGLE-class) extra heads or early exits of the target itself
prompt lookup, n-gram drafting copying from the input: strong when output repeats context

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: lossless, and how much it yields
stages.html:
accept drafted token x with probability  min(1, p_target(x) / p_draft(x))
on rejection, resample from the normalised remainder  max(0, p_target − p_draft)
→ the accepted stream is distributed exactly as the target model's           (Leviathan et al., 2023)

expected tokens per target pass = (1 − α^(k+1)) / (1 − α)        α: acceptance rate, k: drafted tokens

Prove it — tokens per large-model pass for k = 2, 4, 8:

def tokens_per_pass(alpha, k):                  # expected tokens produced per target-model pass
    return round((1 - alpha ** (k + 1)) / (1 - alpha), 2)
for alpha in (0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9):
    print("acceptance", alpha, "→", [tokens_per_pass(alpha, k) for k in (2, 4, 8)])
# → acceptance 0.5 → [1.75, 1.94, 2.0]
# → acceptance 0.7 → [2.19, 2.77, 3.2]
# → acceptance 0.8 → [2.44, 3.36, 4.33]
# → acceptance 0.9 → [2.71, 4.1, 6.13]
Acceptance k = 4 Reading
0.5 1.94 barely two tokens per pass: the draft cost may cancel the gain
0.8 3.36 a clear win
0.9 4.1 predictable text: code, boilerplate, structured output

stages.name: When it breaks
stages.claim: low acceptance or no idle compute
stages.html:
Condition Why it stops paying
large batch, compute saturated verification competes with other requests: throughput falls
mismatched draft model different training or tokenizer: low acceptance
high temperature, creative text high-entropy output is hard to guess
unusual domain the small model hasn't learned it
memory is tight the draft model and its cache need VRAM too

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Tier Setting Why
interactive, small batch on spare compute buys lower TPOT
throughput / batch off compute is the scarce resource there
code, structured output on, with prompt-lookup drafting where output copies input very high acceptance

Metrics: acceptance rate per route, tokens per target pass, TPOT with and without, goodput at the tier's SLO.

Evaluation hook: with exact acceptance, quality is unchanged by construction; a relaxed acceptance rule is an approximation and needs the usual eval.

followUps.question: Why is verifying k tokens about as cheap as generating one?
followUps.html:
Because the weights are read once for the pass, and k tokens share that read.

Weight reads Tokens scored
k normal decode steps k k
one verification pass 1 k

followUps.question: "It's an approximation, so quality drops a little."
followUps.html:
With the standard acceptance rule it is exact.

  • The rule is rejection sampling built so the result follows the target distribution.
  • What changes is wall-clock time and compute used.
  • Only relaxed variants trade quality for more speed.

followUps.question: 🧪 Acceptance 0.7, k = 4. Tokens per target pass?
followUps.html:
About 2.77.

(1 − 0.7⁵) / (1 − 0.7) = (1 − 0.168) / 0.3 ≈ 2.77

followUps.question: How do you choose the draft model?
followUps.html:
Same tokenizer, similar training data, and small enough that its steps are nearly free.

  • Alignment drives acceptance.
  • Size drives the draft cost per token.
  • Measure acceptance on real traffic, per route.

followUps.question: Would you turn it on fleet-wide?
followUps.html:
No: it helps one tier and taxes the other.

Fleet state Effect
light load, small batches lower latency for free
peak load, large batches lower goodput

I'd make it a per-tier setting, and consider switching it off automatically under load.

dontSay: "It reduces computation" — it increases it.
"It's approximate."
"Enable it everywhere."

llm-serving-inference-q12.testing: whether you compare fully loaded cost at real utilisation, and know the requirements that force the decision regardless of cost.
llm-serving-inference-q12.trap: comparing price per token and ignoring utilisation and people.
llm-serving-inference-q12.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "The comparison is not API price against GPU price. It is API price against fully loaded self-hosting: GPUs at their real utilisation, serving engineers, on-call, upgrades, and the evaluation and safety work the provider was doing."
2 · Where the API wins "The API wins on time to market, frontier quality on the hardest tasks, spiky or low traffic, and having no infrastructure team."
3 · Where self-hosting wins "Self-hosting is forced by a few things: data that can't leave the network, deep customisation such as custom fine-tunes or decoding control, a latency floor that needs the model nearby, and independence from a provider's changes. It also wins on cost at high, steady volume."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask first: is there a compliance or control requirement? If not: is utilisation high and steady? A GPU that is ten percent used costs ten times more per token than one fully used."
5 · What I'd pick here "In practice I'd go API-first behind an abstraction layer, and self-host the narrow, high-volume, commodity workloads, such as classification, extraction and embeddings, where a small open model is as good. Then re-run the decision yearly."
Close "A portfolio behind one interface, decided by constraints first and utilisation second."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: fully loaded cost at real utilisation
stages.html:
Cost line API Self-hosted
per token the listed rate GPU cost ÷ (tokens per hour × utilisation)
idle capacity none: pay per use paid for whether used or not
people integration only serving engineers, on-call
upgrades arrive from the provider you evaluate and migrate each new model
safety and eval infrastructure partly included yours to build

stages.name: Where the API wins
stages.html:
Situation Why the API
early product, changing requirements hours to a working version
hardest reasoning tasks frontier models may lead open weights: check on your task
spiky or low traffic no idle GPUs
small team no GPU operations
capability upgrades new models without migration projects of your own

stages.name: Where self-hosting wins
stages.html:
Forcing function Detail
data residency and compliance regulated data that must stay in a network or region
deep customisation custom fine-tunes, constrained decoding, many adapters
latency floor on-premises or edge: no network round trip
strategic independence no silent model updates, no deprecation dates you don't control
cost at steady high volume utilisation stays high around the clock

Hidden costs people skip: GPU on-call, an evaluation pipeline, and re-validating every time a better open model appears.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html: Utilisation is the second question, though. Constraints come first:

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.html:
Workload Likely home Why
classification, extraction, embeddings at high volume self-hosted small models steady load, commodity quality
complex reasoning, low volume provider API frontier quality, no idle cost
regulated data self-hosted or a private deployment residency
burst overflow provider API as fallback elasticity
The abstraction layer:one internal interfaceroutingprovider A, provider B, self-hostedfallbacks tested in advance

Evaluation hook: every candidate home for a workload passes the same eval set before traffic moves.

followUps.question: What goes into "fully loaded"?
followUps.html:
Everything you would stop paying if you switched back to the API.

  • Hardware: GPUs at realistic utilisation, plus spare capacity for failover.
  • People: serving engineering, on-call rotation.
  • Process: evaluation, safety filtering, model upgrades.

followUps.question: "Open-source is free, so self-hosting is cheaper."
followUps.html:
The weights are free; running them is not.

Free Not free
model weights GPUs, idle time, engineers, incidents, migrations

At low or spiky utilisation the API is almost always cheaper.

followUps.question: Traffic is spiky but data must stay in-house.
followUps.html:
Then the constraint wins, and the design absorbs the spikes.

  • A provider's private or in-region deployment, if it satisfies the policy.
  • Self-host with a queue and degradation: a smaller model under load.
  • Shift batch work into the quiet hours to raise utilisation.

followUps.question: What does the abstraction layer need to do?
followUps.html:
Make the model a swappable dependency.

Function Why
one request and response shape callers don't change when the backend does
prompt and model version pinned per route reproducibility
fallback chain with timeouts resilience
per-route cost and quality logging the data for the next decision

followUps.question: How often do you revisit it?
followUps.html:
On a calendar, and on triggers.

Trigger Re-run because
volume crosses a threshold the cost curves may have crossed
a strong new open model the quality gap may have closed
a compliance change a forcing function appeared

Last year's answer expires: model quality, tooling and hardware cost all move.

dontSay: "Self-hosting is cheaper per token" with no utilisation number.
"We prefer open source" — a preference isn't a requirement.
"We'll decide once" — it is a portfolio that shifts.
