llm-serving-inference-q13.testing: whether you route on real difficulty signals, bound the escalation rate, and evaluate each route separately.
llm-serving-inference-q13.trap: routing on prompt length, or reporting one average quality number that hides a broken route.
llm-serving-inference-q13.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask what the task mix is, what a wrong answer costs per task type, and whether there are customer tiers with different guarantees."
2 · Constraints and numbers "Routing pays because difficulty is skewed. If eighty percent of requests are easy and the large model costs twenty times the small one, sending only the hard fifth to it cuts cost from twenty units to under five."
3 · Baseline design "There are two shapes. Pre-routing classifies the request and dispatches it once. A cascade tries the cheap model first and escalates when confidence is low or validation fails. I'd start with static rules by task type, since extraction and open reasoning are obviously different, and add a learned difficulty classifier later."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The hard part is the escalation signal. It has to be something checkable: schema validation, a verifier, token log-probabilities, a retrieval score. And the escalation rate has to be bounded: a cascade that escalates ninety-five percent of requests costs as much as sending everything to the large model, plus latency."
5 · Failure modes "Routing bugs look like random quality complaints from part of the traffic. So every trace carries the route, and quality is measured per route."
6 · Evolve "Later the same idea applies to reasoning budget: thinking tokens only for hard requests."
Close "Cheap by default, escalate on a checkable signal, bound the rate, and evaluate every route separately."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
Ask Why
what task types arrive? some are easy by nature: extraction, classification, short rewrite
what does a wrong answer cost per type? sets how conservative the router is
are there tenant or SLA tiers? a paid tier may always get the larger model
what latency budget? a cascade adds a second call on escalation

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
Prove it — relative cost per request (illustrative: 80% easy, the large model costs 20× the small):

easy, small, big = 0.8, 1, 20                   # share of easy requests; relative cost per request (illustrative)
print("all to big:", big)
print("pre-route:", round(easy * small + (1 - easy) * big, 1))
for esc in (0.2, 0.5, 0.95):                    # cascade: everyone pays the small model, a share escalates
    print("cascade, escalation", esc, "→", round(small + esc * big, 1))
# → all to big: 20
# → pre-route: 4.8
# → cascade, escalation 0.2 → 5.0
# → cascade, escalation 0.5 → 11.0
# → cascade, escalation 0.95 → 20.0
Policy Cost per request Against all-large
everything to the large model 20 —
pre-route, perfect classifier 4.8 76% less
cascade, 20% escalate 5.0 75% less
cascade, 50% escalate 11.0 45% less
cascade, 95% escalate 20.0 no saving, and slower

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
Pre-routing Cascade
Calls per request one one, or two on escalation
Needs a good classifier or clear rules a reliable confidence or validation signal
Latency predictable worse on escalated requests
Pick when task types are distinguishable up front correctness is checkable after the fact

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.claim: a signal you can check, a rate you bound
stages.html:
Signal Good for Weakness
task type (rules) extraction against open reasoning coarse
schema or validator pass/fail structured output only catches format, not wrong content
verifier or judge model free-text answers adds a call
token log-probabilities short answers, classification poorly calibrated on long text
retrieval score RAG: weak context means hard question indirect
learned difficulty classifier mixed traffic needs labelled outcomes; drifts
Bounding escalation:budget per routealert when the rate exceeds itinvestigate the signal, not the budget

Not a signal: prompt length. A long prompt can be a trivial extraction, and a ten-word question can be the hardest request of the day.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Misrouted hard requests quality complaints from a subset of users route ID in every trace; per-route evals
Escalation creep cost rises with flat traffic escalation-rate alert
Model update shifts "easy" a route degrades after a provider change re-run per-route evals on any model change
Average hides a route overall score steady, one route broken report per route, never only the mean
Latency tail escalated requests miss the SLO timeout on the small model; direct-to-large for latency-critical tiers

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Step Adds
learned router trained on logged outcomes: which requests the small model got right
reasoning-budget routing extended thinking only where difficulty warrants it
override path a tenant or a support agent can force the large model
cost and quality per route in every eval report the data to retune thresholds

Fix layer: orchestration. No model changes.

followUps.question: How do you train the difficulty classifier?
followUps.html:
From logged outcomes of the small model.

run both models on a samplelabel where the small one was good enoughtrain a cheap classifier on request featuresvalidate on fresh traffic

followUps.question: "Long prompts go to the big model."
followUps.html:
Length isn't difficulty.

Request Length Difficulty
extract the invoice number from a 20-page PDF long easy
"is this clause enforceable in Germany?" short hard

followUps.question: The small model is confidently wrong.
followUps.html:
Then self-reported confidence can't be the only gate.

  • Use an external check: validator, verifier, retrieval support.
  • Sample confident answers for audit by the large model.
  • Route whole task types away from the small model if audits fail.

followUps.question: How do you evaluate the router itself?
followUps.html:
On cost and quality together, against two baselines.

Compare Reads
all-small the quality floor and cost floor
all-large the quality ceiling and cost ceiling
router should sit near the ceiling's quality at close to the floor's cost

followUps.question: How do you explain a routing change to product?
followUps.html:
As a curve, with the chosen point marked.

  • X axis: share of traffic sent to the large model.
  • Y axis: quality on the eval set.
  • The decision: the smallest share that keeps quality inside the agreed margin, per route.

dontSay: "We route by prompt length."
"Overall quality is unchanged" — per route?
"The cascade escalates when unsure" — unsure by what measure, and how often?

llm-serving-inference-q14.testing: whether you know which tensors are cached, what sharing them costs, and that this is fixed at pre-training.
llm-serving-inference-q14.trap: talking about it as a setting you flip at deployment.
llm-serving-inference-q14.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "At decode time, queries are computed fresh each step; keys and values are what sits in the cache. So the cache size scales with the number of key-value heads. Standard attention gives every head its own. Multi-query shares one across all heads. Grouped-query shares one per group."
2 · Where MQA wins "Multi-query gives the smallest cache: for a seventy-billion-class shape, about forty kilobytes per token against two point six megabytes with full heads. That is sixty-four times less."
3 · Where GQA wins "But sharing a single key-value head costs measurable quality, because every query head must look things up in the same subspace. Grouped-query with eight groups keeps quality close to full attention and is still eight times smaller."
4 · The deciding question "So the question is how much quality you give up per unit of memory, and the answer was settled empirically: most of the saving comes from the first reduction."
5 · What I'd pick here "For me as a serving engineer it isn't a knob. It is baked in when the model is trained, so it is a model-selection criterion: I read it off the model card and it goes straight into my capacity formula."
Close "GQA takes most of the memory win for little quality loss, and I inherit the choice with the model."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: how many K/V heads are cached
stages.html:
MHA GQA MQA
Query heads h h h
Key/value heads h h ÷ group size 1
Cache size largest in between smallest
Quality reference close to reference measurably lower 
KV bytes per token = 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_value      ← the only term that changes

stages.name: Where MQA wins
stages.html:
Prove it — a 70B-class shape (80 layers, 64 query heads, head_dim 128, fp16):

for name, kv_heads in (("MHA", 64), ("GQA 8:1", 8), ("MQA", 1)):
    b = 2 * 80 * kv_heads * 128 * 2             # layers 80, head_dim 128, fp16
    print(name, "|", round(b / 1e6, 3), "MB per token |", round(b * 8192 / 1e9, 2), "GB for an 8k context")
# → MHA | 2.621 MB per token | 21.47 GB for an 8k context
# → GQA 8:1 | 0.328 MB per token | 2.68 GB for an 8k context
# → MQA | 0.041 MB per token | 0.34 GB for an 8k context
Scheme Per token 8k-token context Requests in 40 GB free
MHA 2.62 MB 21.5 GB 1
GQA 8:1 0.33 MB 2.7 GB 15
MQA 0.04 MB 0.34 GB over 100

Less cache also means less memory read per decode step, so TPOT improves too.

stages.name: Where GQA wins
stages.html:
What is shared:many query headsone K/V head per groupeach group looks up in its own subspace
Scheme Lookup diversity Effect
MHA every head has its own keys and values most expressive
GQA several distinct K/V subspaces quality close to MHA (Ainslie et al., 2023)
MQA a single shared subspace all heads retrieve from the same representation: quality dips, training can be less stable

Query-side diversity is preserved in all three: the heads still ask different questions.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Step Memory removed (of the MHA total) Quality cost
MHA → GQA 8:1 87.5% small
GQA → MQA a further 11% larger

The first step buys almost all of the saving. That is why GQA became the usual choice in open-weight models.

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.html:
My role What I can do
choosing a model read num_key_value_heads from the config; prefer GQA models for high-concurrency serving
capacity planning plug kv_heads into the formula
at deployment nothing: the weights were trained with that sharing

Other cache levers I do control: KV-cache quantisation, context limits, paged allocation, prefix sharing.

Why this matters: serving cost now shapes architecture. This is an inference-economics decision made during pre-training.

followUps.question: Why not prune K/V heads after training?
followUps.html:
Because the heads learned to rely on distinct keys and values.

  • Sharing has to be trained in, or carefully up-trained from a checkpoint.
  • Pruning after the fact removes representations the model depends on.

followUps.question: "We'll switch the model to MQA to fit more users."
followUps.html:
There is no switch.

What you can change at serving time What you can't
cache precision, context limits, batch policy the number of K/V heads

To get MQA you would choose, or train, a different model.

followUps.question: 🧪 64 query heads, 16 KV heads. Cache against MHA?
followUps.html:
One quarter.

16 / 64 = 0.25   →   2.62 MB × 0.25 ≈ 0.66 MB per token

followUps.question: Does GQA reduce the number of parameters much?
followUps.html:
Slightly: only the K and V projection matrices shrink.

Affected Not affected
K and V projections Q projections, output projection, MLP blocks

The win is run-time memory and bandwidth, not model size.

followUps.question: How does this enter a model bake-off?
followUps.html:
As a cost column next to quality.

Candidate Eval quality KV MB per token Concurrency per GPU at my context mix
model A measure from config computed
model B measure from config computed

Two models with similar quality can differ several-fold in serving cost.

dontSay: "Enable GQA in the server config."
"MQA is strictly better because the cache is smaller."
"It reduces attention computation" — it reduces what is cached and re-read.

llm-serving-inference-q15.testing: whether you know what a teacher adds beyond labels, and can tie the choice to how many real labels exist and to serving volume.
llm-serving-inference-q15.trap: distilling before checking whether the task needs the large model at all.
llm-serving-inference-q15.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Both end with a small model that is cheap to serve. The difference is the training signal. Fine-tuning learns from human labels. Distillation learns from a large teacher model's outputs."
2 · Where distillation wins "Distillation wins when real labels are scarce and teacher outputs are cheap to generate. The teacher gives more than a label: its probability distribution says a tiger looks a bit like a cat and nothing like a truck. In the LLM setting it usually means the teacher writes the training data and the student is fine-tuned on it."
3 · Where fine-tuning wins "Plain fine-tuning wins when I already have plenty of high-quality labels. Real labels are the ground truth; a teacher's labels include the teacher's mistakes."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask how many good labels I have, and what serving volume will be. Distillation is a one-off training cost against inference that is cheaper for ever, so volume decides whether it pays."
5 · What I'd pick here "My default: teacher generates and labels data, people spot-check it, I fine-tune a small student, and I evaluate the student against the teacher on my task. If the student is inside the agreed margin, it serves; the teacher keeps the hard tail."
Close "Use the teacher when labels are thin, real labels when they aren't, and prove the student against the teacher before it ships."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: where the training signal comes from
stages.html:
Fine-tune a small model Distil into a small model
Signal human labels the teacher's outputs
Needs a labelled dataset a strong teacher and unlabelled inputs
Ceiling label quality and model capacity the teacher's quality
Inherits label noise the teacher's errors and biases
Pick when labels are plentiful and good labels are scarce, the teacher is good

stages.name: Where distillation wins
stages.claim: the teacher says more than a label
stages.html:
Prove it — a teacher's distribution at temperature 1 and 4:

import math
logits = {"tiger": 6.0, "cat": 4.0, "truck": 0.0}       # teacher logits for a picture of a tiger
for T in (1, 4):
    z = sum(math.exp(v / T) for v in logits.values())
    print("T =", T, {k: round(math.exp(v / T) / z, 3) for k, v in logits.items()})
# → T = 1 {'tiger': 0.879, 'cat': 0.119, 'truck': 0.002}
# → T = 4 {'tiger': 0.547, 'cat': 0.331, 'truck': 0.122}
Target What the student is told
one-hot label "tiger", and nothing else
teacher at T = 1 tiger 0.88, cat 0.12, truck ≈ 0
teacher at T = 4 tiger 0.55, cat 0.33, truck 0.12: the ranking of wrong answers becomes visible 
classic loss = α · cross-entropy(student, hard label) + (1 − α) · T² · KL(teacher_T ‖ student_T)
For LLMs, the common form is sequence-level: unlabelled inputsteacher generates outputsfilter and spot-checkfine-tune the student on the pairs

stages.name: Where fine-tuning wins
stages.html:
Situation Why plain fine-tuning
thousands of reviewed, in-domain labels exist nothing for the teacher to add
the teacher is weak on this domain distillation would copy its errors
the task is narrow classification or extraction a small model learns it directly
teacher access is costly or restricted generating data at volume isn't possible, or terms forbid it

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: labels on hand, and volume ahead
stages.html:
distillation pays when:
one-off cost (teacher generation + training + evaluation)  <  (teacher cost − student cost) per request × requests
Labels available Serving volume Choice
many any fine-tune on real labels
few high distil: the one-off cost is recovered quickly
few low keep calling the large model
few, and the task is simple any check first whether the small model already works with a prompt

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.claim: teacher labels, student serves, both compared
stages.html:
Pipeline:sample real inputsteacher labels thempeople audit a samplefine-tune the studentevaluate student against teacherserve
Evaluation Gate
student against teacher, same held-out set within the agreed margin, by slice
student against human labels, where they exist not worse than the teacher
latency and cost per request the saving that justified the project

In production: the student serves the bulk, low-confidence requests go to the teacher, and those become new training data.

followUps.question: Why does temperature matter in classic distillation?
followUps.html:
It flattens the teacher's near-one-hot distribution so small probabilities carry gradient.

T Effect
1 wrong classes are near zero: little to learn from them
higher the relative similarity of classes becomes visible

followUps.question: "Distil first, it always gives a better small model."
followUps.html:
Not if the small model already does the task.

Check first:small model + good promptevaluateonly if it fails, fine-tune or distil

Skipping this is how teams spend a month compressing a model they didn't need.

followUps.question: The student beats the teacher on the eval set.
followUps.html:
Possible on a narrow task; verify before celebrating.

Explanation Check
the student specialised compare by slice, including out-of-distribution inputs
the eval set leaked into training data deduplicate against the generated data
the judge favours the student's style use human labels on a sample

followUps.question: How does this differ from quantising the large model?
followUps.html:
Quantisation shrinks the same model; distillation trains a different, smaller one.

Quantise Distil
Effort hours a training project
Size reduction 2–4× 10× or more is possible
Generality kept yes no: the student is task-specific

followUps.question: Any constraint on using a hosted model as the teacher?
followUps.html:
Yes: check the provider's terms and your data policy.

  • Terms of service may restrict training competing models on outputs.
  • Data policy: inputs sent to the teacher are still subject to residency rules.
  • Record which teacher and prompt produced each training example.

dontSay: "Distillation is always better than fine-tuning."
"The student matches the teacher" — on which slices?
"We'll distil it" before trying the small model with a prompt.

llm-serving-inference-q16.testing: whether you avoid N copies of the weights, and still think about isolation between tenants.
llm-serving-inference-q16.trap: promising per-tenant fine-tunes before asking whether a prompt and retrieval would do.
llm-serving-inference-q16.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "First I'd ask what 'their own model' has to mean. Often the need is tone, terminology and their documents, which a per-tenant prompt and retrieval deliver with no training at all."
2 · Constraints and numbers "If they do need tuned weights, full copies are impossible: three hundred copies of a seventy-billion model is forty-two thousand gigabytes. A rank-sixteen LoRA adapter for the same model is about eighty-four megabytes, so three hundred of them are twenty-five gigabytes."
3 · Baseline design "So the design is one shared base model in GPU memory and a small adapter per tenant, loaded on demand and applied per request. Requests for different adapters can share a batch."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The hard part is the mix of hot and cold tenants. A few tenants carry most traffic: for those I can merge the adapter into a dedicated copy of the base, which removes the per-request overhead. The long tail stays multiplexed, with an in-memory cache of recently used adapters."
5 · Failure modes "Sharing a base doesn't remove isolation work: per-tenant token quotas, caches scoped per tenant, and caps so one tenant can't take the batch."
6 · Evolve "Each adapter is a versioned artefact with its own evaluation, and a base-model upgrade means retraining and re-evaluating all of them."
Close "One base, many small adapters, merge only the hot ones, and isolate tenants at the scheduler."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: do they need weights, or context
stages.html:
What the tenant wants Cheapest thing that delivers it
their terminology, tone, policies a per-tenant system prompt
answers from their documents per-tenant retrieval
a consistent output format schema-constrained output
behaviour a prompt can't produce, or a much shorter prompt at volume a tuned adapter

Only the last row needs per-tenant weights.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
Prove it — LoRA rank 16 on two projection matrices per layer of a 70B-class model:

d, layers, r, tenants = 8192, 80, 16, 300       # 70B-class shape, LoRA rank 16 on two matrices per layer
adapter = 2 * layers * r * (d + d)              # parameters in one adapter
print(adapter, "params |", round(adapter * 2 / 1e6), "MB each in fp16")
print("300 adapters:", round(tenants * adapter * 2 / 1e9, 1), "GB | 300 full copies:", tenants * 140, "GB")
# → 41943040 params | 84 MB each in fp16
# → 300 adapters: 25.2 GB | 300 full copies: 42000 GB

LoRA parameters per matrix = r × (d_in + d_out)
W' = W + (α / r) · B·A          ← the base W is shared; only A and B are per tenant
Approach Memory for 300 tenants
full fine-tuned copies 42,000 GB
one base + 300 adapters 140 GB + 25 GB

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
Property Detail
mixed-adapter batches sequences using different adapters share one base forward pass
hot-swap an adapter loads in seconds, not the minutes a full model takes
storage adapters live in an object store, versioned per tenant

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.claim: hot tenants and the long tail
stages.html:
Unmerged adapter Merged into the base
Per-request overhead a small extra computation per adapted layer none
Memory megabytes per tenant a full base copy per tenant
Switching tenants instant needs another replica
Pick when the long tail the few tenants with steady, high traffic
Tiering:top tenants by trafficmerged, dedicated replicas
Everyone else:shared replicasadapters cached by recent useloaded on demand

Cold adapter: the first request after eviction pays a load. Keep it off the TTFT path by pre-loading on session start, or accept it for rarely active tenants.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.claim: sharing a base is not isolation
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Noisy neighbour one tenant's traffic raises everyone's TTFT per-tenant token limits, fair-share scheduling
Wrong adapter applied tenant A sees tenant B's behaviour adapter ID bound to the authenticated tenant, never to a request field
Shared caches prefix or answer cache leaks across tenants scope caches per tenant
Adapter thrash constant loading and evicting size the cache from the active-tenant count
Throughput drop many distinct adapters in one batch cap adapters per batch; group by adapter where possible

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Concern Practice
per-tenant quality each adapter has its own eval set and release gate
base-model upgrade adapters are tied to the base: retrain and re-evaluate all, roll out per tenant
rollback keep the previous adapter version routable
quantised base adapters trained on the quantised base (QLoRA pattern) are served on it

followUps.question: How can different adapters share a batch?
followUps.html:
The base computation is common; each sequence adds its own low-rank term.

output for sequence i = W·x_i + (α/r) · B_i · (A_i · x_i)        ← W·x for the whole batch at once

followUps.question: "Give every tenant a fine-tuned model."
followUps.html:
Ask what they need before promising weights.

Ladder:promptretrievalfew-shot examplesadapterdedicated model

Each rung costs more to build, evaluate and maintain than the one before.

followUps.question: One tenant's adapter must run in their own region.
followUps.html:
Then that tenant gets a regional deployment, and the design must allow it.

  • Routing by tenant to a regional pool with the same base.
  • Adapter and data stored in-region.
  • Priced accordingly, since a dedicated pool has lower utilisation.

followUps.question: What rank and which layers?
followUps.html:
Small rank on the attention projections is the usual start; evaluate before raising it.

Higher rank Effect
more capacity larger adapters, more overhead per request

followUps.question: How do you price this?
followUps.html:
By the resources each tier actually reserves.

Tier Reserves Price basis
shared, multiplexed adapter tokens used per token
merged, dedicated replica whole GPUs committed capacity

dontSay: "We'll deploy a fine-tuned model per customer."
"LoRA has no serving cost" — unmerged adapters add overhead, and many adapters per batch lowers throughput.
"They share a base, so they're isolated."

llm-serving-inference-q17.testing: whether you have a runtime path for an oversized request, not just advice to avoid one.
llm-serving-inference-q17.trap: "use a model with a bigger context window."
llm-serving-inference-q17.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "They are asking for the runtime path. So: the error should almost never come from the provider, because I count tokens before I call."
2 · Budget before the call "I count with the model's own tokenizer, reserve room for the output, and compare against the limit. If the request doesn't fit, I reduce it deliberately instead of letting the API reject it."
3 · The reduction ladder "Reduction goes in a fixed order, cheapest loss first. Trim the oldest conversation turns. Summarise the history. Drop the lowest-ranked retrieved chunks. If it still doesn't fit, escalate to a longer-context model, or split the work with map-reduce."
4 · What is never cut "Some parts are never truncated silently: the system prompt, the user's actual question, and any source that the answer cites. Cutting those is a correctness bug, not a degradation."
5 · Failure modes "If nothing fits, I return a typed error the caller can act on, and I log the shape of the request: how many tokens each part took."
6 · Evolve "Then I look at why it happened. Repeated overflows on a route mean the context assembly needs a budget per part."
Close "Count first, reduce in a known order, protect what correctness depends on, and fail with a typed error."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: prevention is not the answer they asked for
stages.html:
Where the overflow can be caught Result
before the call, by my own count I choose what to reduce
at the provider a rejected request, latency wasted, nothing chosen
mid-generation (output limit) a truncated answer with finish_reason: length

Two different limits are in play: the context window (input plus output) and the maximum output tokens.

stages.name: Budget before the call
stages.html:
input budget = context limit − reserved output − safety margin
fits  ⇔  tokens(system) + tokens(history) + tokens(retrieved) + tokens(question) ≤ input budget
Rule Why
count with the target model's tokenizer character or word estimates are off by a wide margin for code and non-English
reserve the output first otherwise the answer is the part that gets cut
a budget per part no single component can take the whole window

stages.name: The reduction ladder
stages.html:
The ladder:trim oldest turnssummarise historydrop low-ranked chunkslonger-context modelmap-reducetyped error

Prove it — an 8,000-token limit with 1,000 reserved for output:

limit, reserve_out = 8000, 1000
parts = {"system": 600, "history": 5200, "retrieved": 6000, "question": 150}
budget = limit - reserve_out
total = lambda: sum(parts.values())
print("budget", budget, "| requested", total())
for name, key, new in (("summarise history", "history", 1200), ("drop low-ranked chunks", "retrieved", 4800)):
    if total() > budget:
        parts[key] = new; print(name, "→", total())
print("fits" if total() <= budget else "escalate: longer-context model or map-reduce")
# → budget 7000 | requested 11950
# → summarise history → 7950
# → drop low-ranked chunks → 6750
# → fits
Rung Loses Costs
trim oldest turns old small talk nothing
summarise history detail of earlier turns one cheap model call, cacheable
drop lowest-ranked chunks weakest evidence possible recall loss
longer-context model nothing more cost and latency per request
map-reduce over the input cross-section reasoning several calls

stages.name: What is never cut
stages.html:
Part If silently truncated
system prompt and safety instructions the model's rules change without anyone knowing
the user's current question it answers something else
cited sources the answer cites text the model never saw
tool and schema definitions malformed tool calls
the middle of a document, cut blindly a confident answer from half the evidence

Rule: truncation is an explicit, logged decision on a named part. Never a slice of the final string.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Situation Response
a single input is larger than any window map-reduce, or ask the user to narrow the request
output hit its limit detect finish_reason: length; continue, or tell the user it was cut
nothing can be dropped a typed error: which limit, by how much, which part
an agent loop grew the context compaction step in the loop, with a step limit 
error: context_budget_exceeded   limit=8000   requested=11950   largest_part=retrieved (6000)

A typed error lets the caller retry with fewer documents; a generic 400 does not.

stages.name: Evolve
stages.claim: fix the source, not each overflow
stages.html:
Signal from the logs Structural fix
retrieved context is usually the largest part fewer, better chunks: reranking, smaller chunk size
history dominates in long sessions rolling summary, memory outside the prompt
tool outputs are huge truncate or summarise tool results at the source
one route overflows often a per-part budget enforced in context assembly

Metric: share of requests that needed each rung, per route.

followUps.question: How do you summarise history without losing what matters?
followUps.html:
Keep recent turns verbatim, compress the rest into structured notes.

  • Recent N turns stay as they are.
  • Older turns become a summary of decisions, facts and open items.
  • The summary is cached and extended, not rebuilt each turn.

followUps.question: "Just switch to the model with the million-token window."
followUps.html:
It moves the limit and raises the cost of every request.

Larger window Consequence
more input tokens higher cost and TTFT per request
more KV memory fewer concurrent requests when self-hosted
long contexts accuracy on mid-context details can fall

It is a rung on the ladder, not the first one.

followUps.question: The answer is cut off mid-sentence, but no error was raised.
followUps.html:
That is the output limit, and it reports itself in the finish reason.

check finish_reasonlengthcontinue from the partial output, or raise the output reservationnever show it as complete

followUps.question: How accurate must the token count be?
followUps.html:
Exact for the model in use.

Method Error
characters ÷ 4 large for code, numbers, non-English
the model's tokenizer none, apart from chat-template overhead to add

followUps.question: How do you stop this recurring across teams?
followUps.html:
Put the budget in shared code and in CI.

  • A context-assembly library that enforces per-part budgets.
  • A token-count check in CI for prompt changes.
  • A dashboard of overflow rate and ladder rungs per route.

dontSay: "Use a bigger context window."
"Truncate the prompt to fit" — which part?
"We catch the provider's error and retry" — with the same request?

llm-serving-inference-q18.testing: whether you know a model replica takes minutes to become useful, and that this makes reactive autoscaling too slow by itself.
llm-serving-inference-q18.trap: quoting container start time as the cold-start number.
llm-serving-inference-q18.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "Cold start here means the time from 'I need another replica' to 'it serves its first token at normal speed'. That is minutes, not the seconds a web container takes."
2 · Constraints and numbers "The weights are about a hundred and forty gigabytes in sixteen-bit. Pulled over the network at half a gigabyte a second that is nearly five minutes; from local fast disk at two and a half, under a minute. Then loading into GPU memory and warm-up come on top."
3 · Baseline design "So reactive scaling always lags a spike. I keep a warm pool of loaded replicas, scale predictively from the daily traffic pattern, and never scale interactive traffic to zero."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "To shorten the start itself: keep weights on local disk or a shared cache instead of pulling them, use a format that loads fast, and bake warm-up requests into readiness so the first user doesn't pay for it."
5 · Failure modes "While capacity is arriving, the demand side has to hold: admission control, a queue with backpressure, and degrading to a smaller or quantised model that is already loaded."
6 · Evolve "And I track time-to-ready as a metric, because it sets how much headroom I must keep."
Close "Minutes to start means capacity must be there before the spike, and demand must bend while it arrives."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
A replica's life:node requestedprovisioningpulling weightsloading to VRAMwarmingreadydraining
Phase What happens Typical scale
Provisioning a GPU node is found and booted minutes when none is free
Pulling image and weights fetched the largest term when remote
Loading weights read into GPU memory tens of seconds to minutes
Warming kernels compiled, caches primed seconds to a minute

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
70B parameters × 2 bytes (fp16) = 140 GB                      (throughputs illustrative)
network pull at 0.5 GB/s   →  140 / 0.5 = 280 s
local NVMe at 2.5 GB/s     →  140 / 2.5 =  56 s
int4 copy (35 GB), local   →   35 / 2.5 =  14 s
+ load into VRAM + warm-up, and node provisioning if no GPU is free
Compare Start time
a stateless web container seconds
a 70B model replica minutes

A traffic spike that lasts three minutes is over before a reactive scale-up has helped.

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
Mechanism Does Costs
warm pool loaded replicas held in reserve idle GPU time
predictive or scheduled scaling scale up ahead of the known daily peak needs a traffic pattern
minimum replicas ≥ 1 for interactive tiers no scale-to-zero a baseline cost
headroom target run below full so bursts fit lower utilisation

How much headroom: enough to absorb the growth that can happen during one time-to-ready.

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.html:
Phase Lever
Provisioning pre-provisioned or reserved GPU nodes; node pool kept warm
Pulling weights on local NVMe or a node-level cache; never in the container image layer pulled per start
Loading memory-mappable weight formats; parallel or streamed loading
Warming warm-up requests as part of the readiness check
All a quantised copy: a quarter of the bytes to move
Readiness:process upweights loadedwarm-up generation passesonly then receive traffic

A replica that reports ready before warm-up serves its first real users at cold-path latency.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Scale-up lag TTFT climbs for minutes during a spike warm pool, predictive scaling
Thundering herd onto a new replica it is overloaded the moment it is ready ramp traffic gradually
Queue grows without bound timeouts for everyone admission control, backpressure, 429 with retry-after
No capacity to buy GPU shortage in the region degrade: smaller or quantised model already loaded
Scale-to-zero on an interactive route first user waits minutes minimum replicas
Degradation order:queue brieflyshed batch trafficroute to a smaller modelreject with a clear message

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Metric Use
time-to-ready, per phase shows which phase to attack next
requests served degraded the cost of too little headroom
warm-pool idle hours the cost of too much

Evaluation hook: the fallback model was evaluated on this route's prompts beforehand, or the degradation is a quality incident.

followUps.question: Why not just autoscale faster?
followUps.html:
The floor is physical: bytes have to move.

Faster trigger Still pays
scale on queue depth instead of CPU the full time-to-ready

A better trigger helps by seconds; a warm pool helps by minutes.

followUps.question: "The container starts in 20 seconds, so cold start is 20 seconds."
followUps.html:
The process is up; the model isn't.

container startedweights pulledloaded to VRAMwarmeduseful

Measure to the first token at normal latency.

followUps.question: Traffic is truly bursty and unpredictable.
followUps.html:
Then buy elasticity instead of building it.

  • Overflow to a provider API behind the same interface.
  • A small always-on model takes the burst at lower quality.
  • Queue non-interactive work so it never competes.

followUps.question: Can several models share a warm GPU?
followUps.html:
Yes, at the cost of memory and some interference.

Approach Trade
several small models loaded on one GPU fast switching, less room for KV cache
swap models in and out each swap is a load

followUps.question: How do you justify the cost of a warm pool?
followUps.html:
Against the cost of the minutes it covers.

warm-pool cost = idle replicas × GPU cost per hour
versus          requests degraded or failed during each time-to-ready × their business cost

The pool is sized from the steepest traffic ramp observed, not from the average.

dontSay: "Kubernetes will scale it."
"Cold start is the container start time."
"Scale to zero overnight" for an interactive route.

llm-serving-inference-q19.testing: whether you can name the binding resource, the right scaling signals, and the two things that differ from web servers: slow start and stateful, long-lived requests.
llm-serving-inference-q19.trap: a CPU-based horizontal autoscaler in front of a GPU workload.
llm-serving-inference-q19.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Because CPU isn't the resource that runs out. In LLM serving the binding resource is KV-cache memory and batch slots on the GPU, and CPU utilisation barely moves as those fill."
2 · What load really is "A replica is full when it can't admit another sequence. So the honest signals are queue depth, time waiting for admission, KV-cache occupancy and time-to-first-token violations. Even GPU utilisation misleads, since decode is limited by memory bandwidth."
3 · Prove it "Queueing shows why I scale early. Waiting time grows like utilisation over one minus utilisation: at fifty percent it equals one service time, at ninety it is nine, at ninety-five it is nineteen."
4 · What breaks on scale-down "Two more differences from web servers. A new replica takes minutes to load the weights, so reactive scaling lags. And requests are long-lived and stateful, with their cache on one replica, so scale-down must drain: stop admitting, let streams finish, with a grace period longer than the longest generation."
5 · So what for the system "So I scale on queue and cache signals, predictively with a warm pool, drain on the way down, and use admission control and degradation as the fast levers."
Close "Scale on what actually fills up, start before the spike, and never kill a stream to save a GPU."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
Signal What it measures here Verdict
CPU utilisation tokenisation, networking unrelated to capacity
GPU utilisation compute activity misleading: decode is bandwidth-bound, memory can be full at low utilisation
KV-cache occupancy / free blocks room for another sequence the binding resource
queue depth, admission wait demand exceeding capacity the earliest honest signal
TTFT SLO violations what users feel the outcome to protect

stages.name: What load really is
stages.html:
A replica is "full" when:free KV blocks run outnew sequences wait for admissionqueue growsTTFT rises
Web service LLM serving
requests are short and stateless generations last seconds to minutes and hold state
load ≈ CPU load ≈ KV memory and batch slots
a new replica is useful in seconds useful in minutes
any replica can take any request a session's cache lives on one replica

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: why you scale before it looks busy
stages.html:
queue wait ≈ service time × ρ / (1 − ρ)            ρ: utilisation of the binding resource (single-server model)
Utilisation Wait
0.5 1×
0.8 4×
0.9 9×
0.95 19×

Since a replica takes minutes to arrive, the trigger has to sit well before the steep part.

stages.name: What breaks on scale-down
stages.html:
Wrong:autoscaler removes a replicaprocess killedevery stream on it dies mid-answer
Right:mark drainingstop admittinglet generations finishgrace period > longest streamterminate
Scale-down hazard Control
streams cut mid-generation drain with a grace period sized to the longest allowed generation
cache affinity lost route sessions consistently; accept one re-prefill after a move
flapping long cool-down, since each scale-up costs minutes
batch jobs killed checkpoint, or schedule them on a pool that isn't scaled down mid-job

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Element Choice
scale-out signal queue depth or admission wait, plus KV occupancy
guard signal p95 TTFT against its SLO
timing predictive or scheduled for the daily shape; warm pool for bursts
scale-in slow, with draining
fast levers (seconds) admission control, backpressure, shed batch, degrade to a smaller model
at size separate pools for prefill-heavy and decode-heavy or long-context traffic

Fix layer: capacity and scheduler. The model is untouched.

followUps.question: Which single metric would you scale on if you could pick one?
followUps.html:
Queue wait before admission.

Why Detail
it integrates everything cache pressure, slot pressure and long prefills all show up as waiting
it leads TTFT it rises before the SLO is broken

followUps.question: "GPU utilisation is the GPU equivalent of CPU, scale on that."
followUps.html:
It reports compute activity, and that isn't what runs out.

  • Memory full, compute idle: utilisation low, no room for another request.
  • One long prefill: utilisation high, plenty of memory free.
  • Neither case tells you how many more requests fit.

followUps.question: Traffic doubles in thirty seconds.
followUps.html:
No autoscaler helps in that window, so the demand side does.

First 30 s:admission controlqueue with a boundshed batchdegrade interactive to a smaller model
Meanwhile:warm pool joinsnew replicas load

followUps.question: How long should the drain grace period be?
followUps.html:
Longer than the longest generation the tier allows.

grace ≥ max_output_tokens × p99 TPOT + margin        e.g. 4,000 × 40 ms = 160 s + margin   (illustrative)

followUps.question: What is the cost of scaling this conservatively?
followUps.html:
Idle capacity, which is the price of the SLO.

Choice Pays in
more headroom, warm pool GPU hours
less headroom degraded or late requests during ramps

I'd present both as numbers and let the product owner pick the point.

dontSay: "Put an HPA on CPU."
"GPU utilisation is at 40%, scale down."
"Scale-down just removes a pod."

llm-serving-inference-q20.testing: whether you recognise head-of-line blocking by a long prefill, and fix it in the scheduler and the contract instead of with more replicas.
llm-serving-inference-q20.trap: "add replicas". The blocking moves with the tenant.
llm-serving-inference-q20.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "This is head-of-line blocking. A hundred-thousand-token prefill occupies the GPU for seconds, and every other request on that replica, waiting to start or mid-decode, stalls behind it. The same prompts also take a large share of the KV-cache memory."
2 · Rule out the fakes "I'd first rule out a general capacity shortage, a cold replica, and a prefix-cache regression, since each also raises time to first token."
3 · Confirm with evidence "Then confirm: the spikes should line up in time with that tenant's requests, on the replicas that served them, and show up at p99 while the median stays flat."
4 · Fix by experiment "The first fix is chunked prefill: split the long prompt into pieces and interleave them with other requests' decode steps, so nobody waits for the whole thing. Then structural fixes: token-based rate limits per tenant, and a separate pool for long-context traffic."
5 · Validate "I'd validate with other tenants' p99 time to first token during a replay of that tenant's load."
6 · Productionise "And I'd put a maximum prompt length per tier into the contract, with fair-share scheduling behind it."
Close "A long prefill blocks the line: chunk it, meter it in tokens, and give it its own lane."

stages.name: Name it
stages.claim: a long prefill blocks the line
stages.html:
What happens on the replica:100k-token prompt arrivesone long prefill passdecode steps of other sequences waitnew arrivals queueeveryone's TTFT and TPOT spike
Shared resource How the tenant takes it
compute steps a single prefill holds the GPU for its whole duration
KV-cache memory 100k tokens × 0.33 MB ≈ 33 GB for one request (70B-class, GQA, fp16)

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.claim: other causes of a TTFT tail
stages.html:
Fake How to tell
fleet-wide saturation the tail would not correlate with one tenant's activity
cold or restarting replicas spikes follow deploys or scale events
prefix cache stopped hitting cached-token share dropped at a deploy
slow upstream (retrieval, gateway) the time is outside the model span

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
Observation Likely cause Next action
other tenants' TTFT spikes within seconds of this tenant's requests, same replica head-of-line blocking by prefill enable chunked prefill
admission wait rises while KV free blocks hit zero the tenant's cache footprint per-tenant KV cap, long-context pool
running streams pause mid-answer decode stalled behind the prefill the same
p50 flat, p99 several times higher the blocking is intermittent look at tails per tenant, not the mean

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.html:
Prove it — what chunking changes (illustrative prefill speed):

prefill_ms_per_1k = 60                          # illustrative
prompt, chunk = 100_000, 2_000
print("unchunked: every decode stream stalls once for", prompt // 1000 * prefill_ms_per_1k, "ms")
print("chunked:", prompt // chunk, "pauses of", chunk // 1000 * prefill_ms_per_1k, "ms, one between decode steps")
# → unchunked: every decode stream stalls once for 6000 ms
# → chunked: 50 pauses of 120 ms, one between decode steps
Experiment 1

Chunked prefill

I'd split long prompts into chunks of a few thousand tokens and interleave them with decode steps.

Why? One six-second stall becomes fifty pauses of about a tenth of a second, which other streams hardly notice.

Best suited as the first change: it is a scheduler setting.

Experiment 2

Token-based limits per tenant

I'd meter input tokens per minute per tenant, with a cap on concurrent long prompts.

Why? A request count treats a 100k-token prompt like a 200-token one.

Best suited when a few tenants dominate token volume.

Experiment 3

A long-context pool

I'd route prompts above a threshold to dedicated replicas.

Why? It isolates both the compute and the KV-memory footprint.

Best suited when long-context traffic is steady enough to fill a pool.

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
Metric Before After chunking After pool
other tenants' p99 TTFT measure measure measure
other tenants' p99 inter-token gap measure measure measure
the heavy tenant's own TTFT measure measure: slightly worse measure
goodput of the fleet measure measure measure

The heavy tenant's own latency is allowed to rise a little; that is the trade being made.

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
Layer Control
contract maximum prompt length per tier, stated and enforced at the gateway
gateway token-per-minute limits, concurrent long-request cap, clear 429 responses
scheduler chunked prefill, weighted fair-share across tenants, per-tenant KV cap
capacity long-context pool when volume justifies it
observability TTFT and KV occupancy attributed per tenant
cache safety prefix cache scoped per tenant

followUps.question: What does chunked prefill cost?
followUps.html:
A little latency for the long prompt, and some scheduling overhead.

Chunk size Effect
small smoother for others, longer TTFT for the long prompt
large faster for the long prompt, bigger pauses for others

followUps.question: "Add more replicas."
followUps.html:
Whichever replica receives the long prompt still blocks.

Change Effect on the stall
more replicas it hits a smaller share of users, just as hard
chunking and isolation the stall itself is removed

followUps.question: The tenant is your largest customer and needs 100k prompts.
followUps.html:
Then they get dedicated capacity, priced as such.

  • A reserved pool sized for their long-context load.
  • Prefix caching if their prompts share a stable front, which removes most of the prefill.
  • A check whether retrieval could replace sending everything.

followUps.question: What is evict-and-recompute?
followUps.html:
Freeing a sequence's KV cache under pressure and rebuilding it later by re-running prefill.

memory pressureevict a low-priority sequence's cachelater: re-prefill its tokenscontinue

It is possible because the cache is a deterministic function of the tokens. It costs compute and a pause.

followUps.question: How should the pricing reflect this?
followUps.html:
Charge for tokens and for cache held, not per request.

Unit Reflects
input tokens prefill compute
context-length tier KV memory reserved and time held

Flat per-request pricing makes long-prompt tenants a cost carried by everyone else.

dontSay: "Scale out."
"Rate-limit them to N requests per minute" — requests aren't the unit.
"Average TTFT looks fine."

llm-serving-inference-q21.testing: whether your first move is to split the tail into TTFT and TPOT, and whether you know GPU utilisation says nothing about latency.
llm-serving-inference-q21.trap: reading the utilisation graph and concluding there is headroom, or tuning the model before locating the tail.
llm-serving-inference-q21.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "A wide gap between median and tail with an unsaturated GPU means the slow requests are waiting on something, not computing. Utilisation doesn't tell me what."
2 · Split the metric "First I split it: is the tail in time to first token, or in time per output token, or outside the model server altogether?"
3 · Confirm with evidence "If it is in time to first token, I look at queueing for admission, a cold replica, prefix-cache misses, or a neighbour's long prompt. If it is in time per token, I look at batch contention and at KV-cache pressure forcing preemption and recompute. If the model spans look healthy, the tail is in the gateway, retrieval, tokenisation, or a buffering proxy."
4 · Fix by experiment "The fix follows the location: chunked prefill or admission control for a queueing tail, a batch cap or cache limits for a decode tail, and ordinary service work for anything outside."
5 · Validate "I'd validate on the tail itself: p99 per stage, before and after, on the same traffic."
6 · Productionise "And keep per-stage spans and per-tier percentile SLOs, so next time the answer is a dashboard, not an investigation."
Close "Locate the tail by phase first; only then does a fix make sense."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html:
Prove it — a mean and a median can both look fine while the tail is ten times worse:

lat = sorted([0.4] * 95 + [2.0, 2.2, 2.5, 3.0, 4.0])      # 100 request latencies in seconds (illustrative)
pct = lambda p: lat[min(len(lat) - 1, int(p / 100 * len(lat)))]
print("mean", round(sum(lat) / len(lat), 2), "| p50", pct(50), "| p95", pct(95), "| p99", pct(99))
# → mean 0.52 | p50 0.4 | p95 2.0 | p99 4.0
Statistic Value Says
mean 0.52 s "about half a second"
p50 0.4 s typical request is fast
p95 2.0 s one in twenty is five times slower
p99 4.0 s one in a hundred is ten times slower

An idle-looking GPU with a tail like this means the slow requests spent their time in a queue or a stall.

stages.name: Split the metric
stages.claim: three places a tail can live

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
Observation Phase Likely cause Next action
admission wait high on slow requests TTFT KV memory or slots full at moments admission by free blocks; check long-context traffic
slow requests land on recently started replicas TTFT cold replica, not warmed readiness gated on warm-up
slow requests have a low cached-token share TTFT prefix-cache miss check prompt order and routing affinity
slow requests coincide with one tenant's long prompts TTFT, TPOT head-of-line blocking chunked prefill
gaps mid-stream on slow requests TPOT preemption and recompute under KV pressure per-tenant KV caps, lower concurrency
per-token time rises with batch size TPOT batch contention cap max batch for the tier
model spans normal, total time long outside retrieval, gateway, tokeniser, buffering proxy profile that hop
periodic stalls for all requests outside garbage collection, logging, noisy host host-level metrics

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.claim: one change at the located stage
stages.html:
Experiment 1

Tail in TTFT

I'd enable or tune chunked prefill and admission control, and check warm-up and cache affinity.

Why? Each removes a kind of waiting before the first token.

Best suited when admission wait or prefill dominates the slow traces.

Experiment 2

Tail in TPOT

I'd cap the batch size for the interactive tier and limit KV memory per tenant.

Why? Contention and preemption are what stretch the gaps between tokens.

Best suited when mid-stream pauses appear in the traces.

Experiment 3

Tail outside the model

I'd profile the slow hop: retrieval parameters, connection reuse, proxy buffering.

Why? No model setting fixes time spent elsewhere.

Best suited when model-server spans are healthy.

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
Metric Before After
p99 TTFT measure measure
p99 inter-token gap measure measure
p99 of each non-model hop measure measure
p50 of everything measure measure: must not get worse
goodput measure measure

Compared on the same recorded traffic, since tails depend on the mix.

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
Spans per request:gatewayretrievalqueue waitprefilldecode (with max gap)first byte at client
Practice Why
percentiles per stage, per tier, per tenant a tail is always somebody's
SLOs on p95 or p99, not the mean the mean hid this
alerts on admission wait and preemption count they lead the user-visible tail
GPU utilisation kept off the latency dashboard it invites the wrong conclusion

followUps.question: Why doesn't low GPU utilisation mean spare capacity?
followUps.html:
It measures compute, and the scarce things are memory and bandwidth.

Situation Utilisation Reality
KV cache full low no room for another request
decode at the bandwidth ceiling moderate no faster steps available

followUps.question: "Let's try a faster model to bring p99 down."
followUps.html:
Not before knowing where the time goes.

If the tail is in A faster model
queueing still queues
retrieval or the gateway changes nothing: the model was never the problem

followUps.question: The tail appears only for some users, always the same ones.
followUps.html:
Then it is tied to something those users share.

  • Long conversations: large contexts, more prefill, more cache.
  • A region: an extra network hop or a buffering proxy.
  • A tenant tier: routed to a busier pool.

followUps.question: Which percentile should the SLO use?
followUps.html:
p95 for product targets, p99 for capacity and alerting.

Percentile Use
p50 sanity only
p95 what most users feel on a bad moment
p99 what heavy users hit daily

followUps.question: How do you stop tail investigations taking a week?
followUps.html:
Decide the breakdown before the incident.

  • Standard spans emitted by every service on the path.
  • A tail dashboard that shows slow requests by stage and tenant.
  • A runbook that starts with "TTFT, TPOT, or outside".

dontSay: "The GPU has headroom."
"Average latency is fine."
"Let's add replicas and see."

llm-serving-inference-q22.testing: whether you have an order of attack that starts with measurement and with not calling the model, before any model tuning.
llm-serving-inference-q22.trap: tuning the model server while the latency budget is being spent in retrieval.
llm-serving-inference-q22.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Measure per hop "I'd start with a per-hop latency and cost breakdown, because the slowest hop is rarely the one people assume."
2 · Remove calls "The cheapest optimisation is not calling the model: answer with a rule, a small classifier or a cached response where that is good enough."
3 · Run in parallel "Then I remove sequential work. Retrieval from several sources, independent tool calls and guardrail checks can run at the same time, so the total is the slowest one, not the sum."
4 · Cache at every level "Next, a cache at each level with its own key: the prompt prefix in the model server, embeddings of repeated texts, retrieval results for repeated queries, and whole answers where staleness is tolerable."
5 · Shrink the payload "Then fewer tokens: fewer and better chunks, a tighter prompt, and a hard cap on output length, since output tokens are the slow and costly ones."
6 · Then the model "Only after that the model tier itself: batching settings, quantisation, a smaller model on the easy route. And at the gateway, connection reuse and no response buffering."
Close "Measure, remove, parallelise, cache, shrink, and tune the model last."

stages.name: Measure per hop
stages.html:
Hop Typical waste
gateway new connection per request, buffering
retrieval loose ANN settings, too many candidates
rerank scoring far more candidates than needed
model long prompt, no prefix cache
return path a buffering proxy

stages.name: Remove calls
stages.html:
Request kind Instead of the model
greetings, FAQs, known intents rule or template
routing and classification a small classifier
repeated question cached answer
validation the code can do a schema or regex check, not a second model call
Order of questions:does this need a model?does it need this model?does it need all these tokens?

stages.name: Run in parallel
stages.html:
sequential:  retrieve A 80 ms + retrieve B 120 ms + tool X 150 ms + tool Y 150 ms = 500 ms     (illustrative)
parallel:    max(80, 120, 150, 150)                                              = 150 ms
Can run together Must stay in order
retrieval from several indexes retrieve before rerank
independent tool calls a tool whose input is another's output
input guardrails alongside retrieval output guardrails after generation

Speculative starts also help: begin retrieval while the input guardrail is still checking, and discard if it fails.

stages.name: Cache at every level
stages.html:
Cache Key Saves Risk
prefix (KV) cache exact token prefix prefill time and input cost none for correctness
embedding cache hash of the text and model version an embedding call stale after a model change
retrieval cache normalised query plus filters index lookups stale after the corpus changes
semantic answer cache query embedding within a threshold the whole model call a wrong answer for a near-match; cross-user leakage

stages.name: Shrink the payload
stages.html:
Lever Effect on
fewer, better chunks (rerank, then keep the top few) prefill time, input cost
tighter prompt, stable prefix prefill time, cache hits
truncate tool outputs at the source prefill time
hard cap on output tokens, concise-answer instruction decode time: the dominant term for long answers
structured output instead of prose where the consumer is code decode time 
end to end ≈ TTFT + TPOT × output tokens        ← halving the output halves the second term

stages.name: Then the model
stages.html:
Service Optimisation
gateway connection pooling and keep-alive; streaming with buffering off; timeouts shorter than the user's patience
retrieval tune ANN search effort against recall; pre-filter; smaller candidate set for the reranker
model server continuous batching settings, prefix caching, quantisation, a smaller model on easy routes
post-processing validate incrementally on the stream instead of after it

Evaluation hook: every latency change is paired with a quality check on the eval set, since shrinking context and routing down can cost quality.

followUps.question: Which single change usually gives the most?
followUps.html:
It depends on the breakdown, which is why it comes first.

Largest term Usual best lever
output generation cap and shorten the output
prefill prefix caching, less context
retrieval or rerank fewer candidates, tuned search

followUps.question: "Use a faster model."
followUps.html:
It helps only the model's share of the time.

model share 25% of latency, model made 2× faster  →  total improves by 12.5%

followUps.question: Everything is already parallel and cached. Still slow.
followUps.html:
Then change what the user waits for.

  • Stream so the first token arrives early.
  • Show progress for multi-step work.
  • Move work off the request path: precompute, summarise at ingestion.

followUps.question: How do you keep a semantic cache safe?
followUps.html:
Tight threshold, scoped keys, and an expiry.

  • Scope by tenant and by anything that changes the answer: user, locale, permissions.
  • Invalidate when source documents change.
  • Audit a sample of hits for wrong matches.

followUps.question: When is horizontal scaling the right answer after all?
followUps.html:
When per-request work is already lean and the queue is the problem.

Symptom Answer
each request is slow even alone optimise the path
requests are fast alone, slow under load capacity or scheduling

dontSay: "We'd tune the model server" as the first step.
"Add a cache" — which one, keyed on what?
"It's the LLM that's slow" without a breakdown.

llm-serving-inference-q23.testing: whether you share the fleet with priority classes so batch absorbs the slack, instead of paying for two peaks.
llm-serving-inference-q23.trap: two static clusters, one per workload.
llm-serving-inference-q23.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd confirm the two SLOs. Chat needs a p95 time to first token, say under a second, and peaks during the day. The bulk API needs a completion deadline, say by morning, and doesn't care about first-token time."
2 · Constraints and numbers "The point of sharing is that their demands are complementary. Chat capacity sized for the daytime peak sits idle at night. Two separate clusters pay for both peaks; one shared pool pays for the larger one."
3 · Baseline design "So: one pool, two priority classes. Chat requests are admitted first, with a small batch cap, chunked prefill and streaming. Bulk requests come from an offline queue, run in large batches, and fill whatever capacity chat isn't using."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The hard part is making bulk yield quickly. When chat load rises, the scheduler stops admitting bulk sequences, and can preempt running ones: evict their cache and requeue them. Bulk work is idempotent and resumable, so preemption costs compute, not correctness."
5 · Failure modes "The failures are bulk starving and missing its deadline, and bulk's large batches leaking into chat latency."
6 · Evolve "I'd reserve a minimum share for bulk, and split into separate pools only if measured interference justifies it."
Close "Tiers on one pool: chat preempts, batch absorbs the slack, and the deadline gets a guaranteed floor."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
Chat Bulk document API
SLO p95 TTFT, then a minimum token rate job completes before a deadline
Traffic shape daytime peak, bursty steady or scheduled; deferrable
Request shape short prompt, streamed answer long prompt, often short output
Tolerates nothing visible queueing, preemption, retries
Optimise for latency throughput

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
chat peak needs 20 GPUs (day), 4 at night          bulk needs 10 GPU-equivalents, any time     (illustrative)
two static clusters:  20 + 10 = 30 GPUs
shared pool:          20 GPUs  → bulk uses the 16 idle at night, plus daytime slack
Design GPUs Idle capacity
two clusters 30 chat cluster mostly idle at night
one pool with tiers 20 filled by bulk

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
Setting Chat tier Bulk tier
admission immediate only when chat headroom is intact
batching small cap to protect TPOT as large as memory allows
prefill normal chunked, so it never blocks chat
delivery streaming results written to a store
under pressure protected shed or preempted first

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.html:
When chat load rises:stop admitting bulklet short bulk sequences finishpreempt long ones: evict KV cache, requeuechat takes the slots
Requirement on bulk work Why
idempotent items with an ID a requeued item can't be processed twice into the output
per-item checkpointing a preempted job resumes, not restarts
long prompts chunked a bulk prefill never stalls a chat stream
output is not streamed to a person a restart is invisible

Headroom rule: bulk may use capacity only down to a reserve that covers chat's fastest observed ramp, because new replicas take minutes.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
Bulk starves deadline missed on a busy day a guaranteed minimum share; escalate priority as the deadline nears
Bulk leaks into chat latency chat TPOT rises when bulk is running separate batch caps; verify with chat p95 while bulk is on
Preemption thrash bulk makes no progress minimum run time before preemption; fewer, longer windows
Chat spike beyond the pool TTFT SLO broken autoscale on queue wait; degrade to a smaller model
KV memory taken by bulk chat admission waits per-tier KV caps

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Signal Then
chat p95 is unaffected by bulk keep one pool
measured interference remains after caps dedicate a few replicas to chat, share the rest
bulk prompts are far longer than chat a prefill-heavy pool for bulk
bulk volume grows past the night-time slack add capacity sized for the deadline, not for latency

Metrics: chat p95 TTFT with and without bulk running; bulk completion time against deadline; fleet goodput; preemption count.

followUps.question: Why not just two clusters? It is simpler.
followUps.html:
Simpler, and you pay for the peak of each.

Two clusters Shared with tiers
GPUs sum of the peaks the larger peak
Idle time high low
Complexity low a scheduler with priorities

I'd only split once interference is measured and can't be tuned away.

followUps.question: How is preemption implemented safely?
followUps.html:
Evict the cache, requeue the item, recompute on resume.

preemptfree KV blocksitem returns to the queue with its progresslater: re-prefill and continue

It is safe because the cache can be rebuilt from the tokens.

followUps.question: The bulk deadline is in two hours and chat is at peak.
followUps.html:
The deadline raises bulk's priority, within limits agreed beforehand.

  • Escalate bulk to its guaranteed share.
  • Add capacity for the window, or overflow bulk to a provider's batch API.
  • Tell the bulk customer the expected completion time, not silence.

followUps.question: Should bulk use a different model configuration?
followUps.html:
It can use different serving settings on the same weights.

Setting Bulk
speculative decoding off: compute is the scarce resource
max batch high
output capped and structured

followUps.question: How do you charge the two workloads?
followUps.html:
By the guarantee each one buys.

Tier Buys Price
chat reserved, latency-protected capacity higher per token
bulk preemptible leftover capacity with a deadline lower per token

dontSay: "Two clusters, one each."
"Batch runs at night" — and when chat is busy at night in another time zone?
"Chat gets priority" with no floor for the deadline.

llm-serving-inference-q24.testing: whether you start with token accounting per route and apply levers in order of leverage, before any talk of hardware.
llm-serving-inference-q24.trap: starting with GPU shopping or a cheaper provider.
llm-serving-inference-q24.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "Cost is requests times tokens per request times cost per token. A bill that is out of control means one of those three moved, usually on one feature, not everywhere."
2 · Attribute the spend "So first I attribute spend per route from trace data. Typically a small share of requests carries a large share of cost: in my example a summarisation feature is five percent of requests and nearly half the spend."
3 · Confirm with evidence "Then I check the usual suspects: a prompt edit that broke prefix caching, context that grew, outputs that got longer, an agent looping more, or a routing change sending more traffic to the expensive model."
4 · Fix by experiment "I cut in order of leverage. Don't call the model where a rule or cache will do. Cache the prefix. Route easy requests down. Shorten the context and cap the output, since output tokens cost several times input tokens. Only then quantise or self-host."
5 · Validate "Each cut is checked against quality on the eval set and against cost per successful task, not just cost per request."
6 · Productionise "And I add budgets per tenant, a cost alert per route, and a token check in CI for prompt changes."
Close "Account per route, remove and cache before you tune, and put the budget in before the invoice."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html:
cost = requests × tokens per request × cost per token
       └ traffic ┘  └ prompt, context, output ┘  └ model choice, cache hits ┘
Factor Moves when
requests traffic grows, retries multiply, agents loop
tokens per request context bloat, more chunks, longer outputs, bigger tool results
cost per token route mix shifts to a pricier model; a cache stops hitting

stages.name: Attribute the spend
stages.html:
Prove it — three routes, 1M requests a day (illustrative token counts; an output token weighted 4× an input token):

routes = {"chat": (600_000, 1_800, 250), "summarise": (50_000, 30_000, 800), "classify": (350_000, 400, 5)}
out_weight = 4                                   # one output token costs a few input tokens (illustrative ratio)
cost = {r: n * (i + out_weight * o) for r, (n, i, o) in routes.items()}     # requests/day, input tokens, output tokens
total = sum(cost.values())
for r, c in sorted(cost.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
    print(r, "|", round(100 * c / total), "% of spend |", round(100 * routes[r][0] / 1_000_000), "% of requests")
# → chat | 48 % of spend | 60 % of requests
# → summarise | 48 % of spend | 5 % of requests
# → classify | 4 % of spend | 35 % of requests

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
Observation Likely cause Next action
cached-token share fell on a deploy date a prompt edit changed the prefix restore a stable prefix; move volatile content to the end
input tokens per request rising over weeks context bloat: more chunks, longer history cap chunks, compact history
output tokens per request rose prompt change invited longer answers; no cap cap max_tokens, ask for concise output
requests per user session rose agent loop iterating more, or client retries step limit, retry budget
share of traffic on the expensive model rose routing regression per-route evals, fix the router
one tenant dominates no quota per-tenant budget

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.html:
The order:don't callcacheroute downshorten tokenscap outputbatch API for offline workquantise or self-host
Experiment 1

Restore prefix caching

I'd make the system prompt and tool definitions byte-stable and move volatile fields to the end.

Why? It is often a one-line change that removes most of the input cost on every request.

Best suited when the cached-token share is low or recently dropped.

Experiment 2

Route down the easy traffic

I'd send classification and simple extraction to a small model.

Why? Those routes don't need the large model, and the saving scales with their volume.

Best suited when a route passes the eval set on the small model.

Experiment 3

Cut tokens on the expensive route

I'd reduce context and cap output on the summarisation route, and move it to a batch API if it isn't interactive.

Why? That one route is half the bill.

Best suited when a single route dominates spend.

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
Metric Before After
cost per successful task, per route measure measure
quality on the eval set, per route measure measure: within margin
cached-token share measure measure
input and output tokens per request measure measure
retry and re-ask rate measure measure: must not rise

A cheaper answer that users have to ask for twice is not cheaper.

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
Control Catches
per-tenant and per-route budgets with circuit breakers runaway usage, the same day
cost-per-task alert on the slope gradual drift
token-count check in CI for prompt changes a pull request that doubles tokens
cost column in every eval report quality gains that cost too much
step and retry limits on agents loops

followUps.question: Traffic is flat and the bill doubled. What changed?
followUps.html:
Tokens per request or cost per token.

Suspect Check
prefix cache broke cached-token share over time
context or output grew tokens per request over time
route mix shifted share of requests per model

followUps.question: "Let's negotiate a discount or switch provider."
followUps.html:
That trims a percentage; the waste is usually a multiple.

Move Result
discount or new provider the same wasted tokens, slightly cheaper
accounting first the wasted tokens are removed, then you negotiate on what is left

followUps.question: The expensive route is the one customers value most.
followUps.html:
Then cut its waste, not its quality.

  • Prefix caching and tighter context don't change the answer.
  • Batch processing for the non-interactive part.
  • Price it to reflect its cost, if it is a premium feature.

followUps.question: Why do output tokens matter more?
followUps.html:
Each one is a separate decode step, while input tokens share one prefill pass.

Input tokens Output tokens
Processed in parallel one per step
Typical cost weight 1× several ×

followUps.question: When does self-hosting become the right cut?
followUps.html:
Last, and only for steady, high-volume routes that pass on an open model.

Precondition Why
the waste is already removed otherwise you self-host the waste
utilisation will be high idle GPUs cost more than the API
an open model passes the eval or quality pays for the saving

dontSay: "Buy cheaper GPUs" or "switch to a cheaper model" as the opening move.
"Total spend is X" — per route?
"We cut cost 40%" with no quality number beside it.

llm-serving-inference-q25.testing: whether you measured before changing anything, can name the metric you moved, and can say what you rejected and what regressed.
llm-serving-inference-q25.trap: a fix with no before-number. It reads as a guess that happened to work.
llm-serving-inference-q25.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision it served "At Velocit AI I worked on VhAIre, an AI interviewer that talks to candidates by voice. The inference path I'll describe is one conversational turn: speech in, a model response, speech out."
2 · The constraint "Turn-taking under about a second is the product. Above that the conversation stops feeling human, so the latency of the model call sat directly on the user experience."
3 · Options weighed "I measured the turn stage by stage first. <fill: what the per-stage breakdown showed, and which stage you had assumed was slow>. The options were one large model call per turn against a LangGraph state machine with smaller steps, and a higher-quality model against a faster provider for latency-critical turns."
4 · What I built "<fill: what you chose and the deciding factor; which turn types went to the fast model and which to the stronger one>. I rejected <fill: the lever you decided against, and why>."
5 · What broke "It wasn't free. <fill: what regressed or broke in production, and what you changed after>."
6 · The number "The result: turn latency went from <fill: p50 / p95 before> to <fill: p50 / p95 after>, measured <fill: how and over what traffic>."
Close "What I'd take from it: split the latency by stage before choosing a lever, and route by what each turn actually needs."

stages.html:
Turn type Routed to Why
<fill: e.g. acknowledgements, short follow-ups> <fill> <fill>
<fill: e.g. evaluation or probing questions> <fill> <fill>
Other levers Used?

llm-serving-inference-q26.testing: whether you see the model call as one box among many, and can say what each surrounding layer is for.
llm-serving-inference-q26.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask who the users are, whether it is multi-tenant, what data the model may see, and whether model output triggers actions. Those decide how heavy each layer needs to be."
2 · Constraints and numbers "I'd set a budget per request: latency to first token, input and output tokens, and a cost ceiling. Each layer gets a share."
3 · Baseline design "On the way in: a gateway for authentication and per-tenant token limits; input guardrails for moderation, injection screening and PII; context assembly, which is retrieval, memory, examples and tool schemas; and a router that picks the model. In the middle: a provider abstraction with timeouts, retries, fallbacks and pinned prompt and model versions. On the way out: output validation, then streaming to the client."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The part teams skip is the provider abstraction. It makes the model a swappable dependency: one internal interface, several backends, and fallbacks that were tested with the same prompts and evals in advance."
5 · Failure modes "Cutting across everything: caching at several levels, tracing with prompt version, tokens, cost and latency per span, and budget enforcement per tenant."
6 · Evolve "And an evaluation pipeline wired to production traffic, so every change to any layer is measured."
Close "Reliability, cost and iteration speed live in this scaffolding; the model is one swappable box in it."
