llm-serving-inference-q27.testing: whether you treat output quality as a production metric, and alert on rates and drift instead of single events.
llm-serving-inference-q27.trap: "we log prompts and responses and have latency dashboards."
llm-serving-inference-q27.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "The difference from classical monitoring is that a request can succeed technically and still be wrong. So quality has to be observed in production, and behaviour can change without a deploy when a provider updates a model."
2 · What to capture "Per request I capture a trace: prompt version, model and parameters, retrieved context IDs, tool calls, token counts, cost, and latency split into time to first token and time per token. Metadata for every request; payloads sampled and redacted."
3 · Quality as a signal "On top of that, quality proxies: schema-validation failures, guardrail triggers, refusal rate, groundedness or judge scores on a sampled stream, and user signals such as regenerations, edits and thumbs."
4 · What to alert on "I alert on rates and slopes: a spike in validation failures, a jump in refusals, cost per task trending up, a drop in cached-token share, a shift in route mix, and p99 time-to-first-token breaches."
5 · Failure modes "The risks are logging private content, sampling so little that tails vanish, and dashboards that can't be sliced by prompt and model version."
6 · Close the loop "Finally, flagged traces go to a review queue and become eval cases, so the monitoring feeds the next release gate."
Close "Trace with versions and token economics, score a sample for quality, and alert on drift you didn't deploy."

llm-serving-inference-q28.testing: whether you limit tokens instead of requests, handle the fact that output size is unknown at admission, and separate platform protection from fairness between tenants.
llm-serving-inference-q28.trap: "100 requests per minute per API key."
llm-serving-inference-q28.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "The first difference is the unit. One request can be a hundred tokens or a hundred thousand, so a request count says almost nothing about load."
2 · Constraints and numbers "So I limit tokens per minute, input and output separately since they cost differently, alongside a request limit. A token bucket works directly, with model tokens as the currency."
3 · Baseline design "At the gateway each tenant has buckets for input tokens, output tokens and requests, plus a monthly quota. A rejected call gets a 429 with a retry-after and headers showing what is left."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The hard part is that output tokens aren't known when I admit the request. I reserve the declared maximum output, then reconcile to the actual usage when the stream ends. Without that, a tenant can exceed its budget in the middle of a stream."
5 · Failure modes "The second difference is the noisy neighbour. Capacity is batch slots and KV memory, so one tenant's long-context burst raises everyone's time to first token even inside its rate limit. That needs fair-share scheduling and a cap on concurrent long requests, not just a rate."
6 · Evolve "Before rejecting, I'd offer degradation: queue it, or route to a smaller model if the tenant has agreed."
Close "Rate limits protect the platform; fair scheduling protects tenants from each other; both are counted in tokens."

Scarce resource CPU, connections batch slots, KV memory, token throughput

Right unit requests per second tokens per minute, plus concurrency

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.claim: a token bucket in model tokens
stages.html:
Prove it — 60,000 tokens per minute with a burst of 6,000:

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate, cap): self.rate, self.cap, self.level, self.t = rate, cap, cap, 0.0
    def allow(self, now, tokens):
        self.level = min(self.cap, self.level + (now - self.t) * self.rate); self.t = now
        if tokens > self.level: return False
        self.level -= tokens; return True
b = TokenBucket(rate=1000, cap=6000)             # 60,000 model tokens per minute, burst of 6,000
print([b.allow(t, n) for t, n in [(0, 4000), (1, 4000), (2, 500), (5, 4000)]])
# → [True, False, True, True]
Time Asked Bucket before Decision
0 s 4,000 6,000 allowed
1 s 4,000 3,000 rejected: only 1,000 refilled
2 s 500 4,000 allowed
5 s 4,000 6,000 (capped) allowed 
refill rate = tokens per minute / 60        capacity = allowed burst

stages.html:

Long-context burst inside the rate limit everyone's TTFT rises concurrent long-request cap; chunked prefill; long-context pool (gateway, scheduler, capacity)
One tenant fills the queue others wait behind it weighted fair queueing per tenant (scheduler)

Limits per API key, not per tenant a tenant multiplies keys aggregate at the tenant (gateway)

followUps.html:
A request count can't tell a 200-token call from a 100,000-token one.

10 requests × 200 tokens = 2,000 tokens          10 requests × 100,000 tokens = 1,000,000 tokens

Same count, five hundred times the load.

followUps.html:

Purpose Cached tokens

maximum context and KV memory counted fully: they still occupy cache

followUps.html:
Enough for a client to pace itself without guessing.

  • Limit, remaining and reset time for requests and for tokens.
  • Retry-After on a 429.
  • A machine-readable reason: rate, quota, or size.

followUps.html:

llm-serving-inference-q29.testing: whether you separate the three failure types and have a defence for each that was built and tested before the incident.
llm-serving-inference-q29.trap: "we retry" for all three, or a fallback model that was never evaluated.
llm-serving-inference-q29.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "There are three different failures in that question: availability, capacity or latency, and behaviour. Each needs its own defence, built in advance."
2 · Availability failures "For intermittent overload errors: retries with exponential backoff and jitter, under a retry budget so they can't amplify the outage. A circuit breaker per provider stops calling one that is failing. Behind it, a fallback chain: another provider, a smaller model, a cached or templated response."
3 · Latency degradation "For slowness: timeouts shorter than the user's patience, streaming so partial progress shows, a bounded queue with backpressure, and shedding load into a degraded mode instead of letting requests pile up."
4 · Silent behaviour change "For the silent update: pin model versions wherever the provider allows it. Where it doesn't, the tripwires are validation-failure rate and eval scores on sampled production traffic, because drift shows up there first."
5 · Failure modes "The fallback is only real if the prompts and evals were run on the fallback model beforehand. An untested fallback turns an outage into a quality incident."
6 · Evolve "And the degradation ladder is a product decision made in advance: full capability, smaller model, cached answers, an honest unavailable message."
Close "A hosted model is a critical dependency I don't control, so the resilience exists before the bad day."

stages.claim: retry carefully, then stop, then fall back
stages.html:
Prove it — a backoff schedule with jitter, and what unbudgeted retries do:

import random
random.seed(1)
delays = [round(min(8, 0.5 * 2 ** n) * random.uniform(0.5, 1), 2) for n in range(5)]
print(delays, "| total wait", round(sum(delays), 2), "s")
print("3 layers each retrying 3 times:", 3 ** 3, "calls for one user request")
# → [0.28, 0.92, 1.76, 2.51, 5.98] | total wait 11.45 s
# → 3 layers each retrying 3 times: 27 calls for one user request

retry only on retryable errors; exponential backoff with jitter; honour Retry-After
retry budget a cap on retries as a share of traffic, set at one layer only
circuit breaker per provider and model; open means fail fast to the fallback
fallback chain alternate provider ─▶ smaller model ─▶ cached or templated response
idempotency key a retried request must not act or bill twice

llm-serving-inference-q30.testing: whether you recognise static batching from the symptom pair "idle GPU, growing queue", and fix the scheduler and the memory allocator instead of adding GPUs.
llm-serving-inference-q30.trap: "raise the batch size to 32", or "add more GPUs".
llm-serving-inference-q30.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "Idle GPUs with a growing queue means work exists but the server isn't admitting it. A hard-coded batch of eight points at static batching: each batch runs until its longest sequence ends, so finished slots sit empty while new requests wait."
2 · Rule out the fakes "I'd rule out a bottleneck in front of the GPU, such as slow tokenisation or a single-threaded preprocessing step, and memory being full."
3 · Confirm with evidence "To confirm: per-slot activity should show most slots idle for most of each batch, and queue wait should track the longest generation in the batch."
4 · Fix by experiment "The fix is continuous batching: admit and evict every decode step, so a freed slot is refilled at once. Then paged KV-cache allocation, so memory isn't reserved for the maximum length and the batch can grow past eight. And chunked prefill, so a long new prompt doesn't stall the running streams."
5 · Validate "I'd validate on tokens per second per GPU, time to first token and the gap between tokens, since batching trades the last for the first."
6 · Productionise "In practice this means moving to an inference server that does this, and setting the maximum batch from the latency SLO instead of a constant."
Close "The GPU was waiting on the slowest sequence; schedule per step and page the cache, and the idle time becomes throughput."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html:
Static batch of 8:8 requests start togethershort ones finish earlytheir slots idlebatch ends when the longest finishesnext 8 admitted
Symptom Explained by
low GPU utilisation most slots are empty for most of each batch
queue grows new requests wait for the whole batch to finish
latency of short requests is high they wait for the longest, twice: in the queue and, if results return together, in the batch

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html:
Fake How to tell
CPU-side bottleneck (tokenisation, pre-processing, Python GIL) CPU saturated; GPU waits between batches
slow input or output path time is in network or disk spans
KV memory full free memory near zero; admission blocked by memory, not by the batch constant
queue is in another service the model server's own queue is empty

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
Prove it — twelve requests of mixed length on four slots:

lengths = [20, 200, 30, 180, 25, 190, 40, 210, 35, 15, 220, 45]     # output tokens per request
B = 4                                                              # batch slots
static = sum(max(lengths[i:i + B]) for i in range(0, len(lengths), B))   # each batch runs until its longest ends
slots = [0] * B                                                    # continuous: a freed slot is refilled at once
for n in lengths:
    i = slots.index(min(slots)); slots[i] += n
continuous = max(slots)
useful = sum(lengths)
print("static:", static, "steps, slot use", round(useful / (static * B), 2))
print("continuous:", continuous, "steps, slot use", round(useful / (continuous * B), 2))
# → static: 630 steps, slot use 0.48
# → continuous: 435 steps, slot use 0.7
Observation Likely cause Next action

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.html:
Experiment 1

Continuous batching

I'd switch the scheduler to admit and evict sequences at every decode step.

Why? A finished sequence's slot is reused immediately, so slots stop idling behind the longest sequence.

Best suited when output lengths vary, which is always the case in chat.

Experiment 2

Paged KV-cache allocation

I'd allocate the cache in fixed-size blocks on demand instead of a maximum-length region per request.

Why? Worst-case reservation is what capped the batch at eight; paging lets the batch grow to what memory really holds.

Best suited when most requests are far shorter than the maximum context.

Experiment 3

Chunked prefill

I'd split long incoming prompts and interleave the chunks with decode steps.

Why? With a dynamic batch, an unchunked long prefill would stall every in-flight stream.

Best suited as soon as continuous batching is on.

Fix layer: scheduler and allocator. No model change and no new hardware.

followUps.question: Why does a bigger batch help decode at all?
followUps.html:
Decode is bandwidth-bound: the weights are read once per step whatever the batch.

Batch Weight reads per step Tokens per step
8 1 8
32 1 32

More sequences share the same memory traffic.

followUps.question: "Just raise the hard-coded batch to 32."
followUps.html:
A bigger static batch waits even longer for its slowest member.

Static batch Effect
larger more requests held until the longest finishes; more padding; more memory reserved

The problem is that the batch is static, not that it is small.

followUps.question: All requests produce exactly 100 tokens. Is static batching fine then?
followUps.html:
Much closer to fine, if they also arrive together.

Workload Static batching
uniform length, offline little slot waste
uniform length, arriving at random requests still wait for a batch to form

followUps.question: After the fix, utilisation is still only 40%.
followUps.html:
That can be a healthy decode workload.

  • Decode is limited by bandwidth, so compute utilisation stays moderate.
  • Check tokens per second, queue wait and free KV blocks instead.

followUps.question: How would you have caught this before production?
followUps.html:
A load test with realistic length variance and a goodput target.

  • Replay recorded traffic, not uniform synthetic prompts.
  • Report goodput at the SLO, slot occupancy and queue wait.
  • Compare against a known server as a baseline.

dontSay: "Add GPUs" — the ones you have are 85% idle.
"Increase the batch size."
"Utilisation is low, so the model is the bottleneck."
